speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I owe an apology to certain hon. members of this house in respect of the arrangements made for the sittings of the house, and I should like to make that apology publicly. These hon. members have called to my attention some ambiguity in the language I used here on Tuesday, as reported on page 2 of Hansard, and told me they took it to mean that I was not asking that the house sit tomorrow if the bill dealing with the resumption of railway operations was disposed of.
I am sorry there was any misunderstanding as to that. In speaking as I did on Tuesday I was not trying to impose upon the house my views as to what might be the best way to proceed, but was endeavouring to get something definite which would represent what was generally desired by the members of the house. On Monday I had drafted a certain motion in that regard, and Monday evening had the advantage of meeting with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leaders of the other groups, to whom I gave copies of the draft motion which had been prepared. The next day representations were made to me that hon. members probably would not be prepared to commit themselves to three sittings a day beyond the time required to dispose of the railway legislation. I was under the impression that that was the only point in the draft motion to which any exception was apt to be taken, and I had the motion redrafted to provide that the three sittings a day would continue only during the time required to deal with the railway legislation; and I made no other change.
When I spoke as is reported on page 2 of Hansard, the only thing I had in mind was to 09 262-8i
point out that this objection to three sittings a day had been taken and that the motion originally prepared had been intended to provide three sittings even on Saturday, but that I had taken out that provision except for the railway bill. Some hon. members have told me they were under the impression that
1	had taken out everything beyond the provision of the rules for normal sittings, and that I would have to ask the house for another commitment to do anything beyond that. I did not realize this. When I presented the motion I read it as it appears on page 4 of Hansard, and I was under the impression that its terms were understood by everyone. I am told that it was not thus understood by certain hon. members. I am very sorry there was any possibility of ambiguity in the language that appears on page 2 of Hansard, and certainly I do not want to appear to be taking advantage of any misunderstanding. I would hope that if anyone wished again to take the sense of the house on this question, you, Mr. Speaker, would permit that to be done. Naturally I would hope that the decision might be the same and that we would sit tomorrow and Monday. As a matter of fact I had another conference with the leaders yesterday morning, at which we discussed whether or not it would be appropriate to sit on Monday, and I believe my recollection is correct that it was agreed that since we were sitting on Saturday it would be just as well to sit on Monday, since that is what we usually do on legal holidays, except those having high religious significance. So I would hope that even if the question is put again the same conclusion might be reached, because I think a great many hope that at this special session we might be able to dispose next week of all that requires to be done, and not too hurriedly at that; for this is by no means the last time parliament will meet. But so that there may be no possible feeling that anyone is being held to something that he did not understand, if any hon. member wishes to have the sense of the house expressed again I would hope, Mr. Speaker, you would find it possible to allow that to be done.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, August 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Charles Cannon for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this session was called to consider two urgent and extremely important matters. One was the railway strike and the way in which the railways could be brought back into operation. The other was the international situation and the organization for defence which that situation imposes upon us. Both were matters calling for immediate consideration. The speech from the throne is simply an agenda indicating the two important subjects that are to be discussed. The first has been disposed of. In disposing of it, because of the urgency and also, I am inclined to think, because of the fact that the speech from the throne did no more than indicate the subject matter, the debate on the speech from the throne was postponed so that hon. members might deal immediately with the operative provision


being made by the government to deal with this situation. The legislation to restore the operation of the railways was brought before us and was dealt with. That seemed to meet with the general approval of the members of this house.
We now have another urgent matter to consider; and in many ways it is an even more important matter in its ultimate implications. There again in the speech from the throne we have nothing but a reference to the subject matter. We have no information as to the details that are to be placed before us, and we are therefore not in a position at the moment to say what the government has indicated it intends to do or does not intend to do, beyond the mere fact that the matter is to be brought before us.
It seemed to me that, following the procedure which had been adopted in dealing with the railway strike, it would be better that the debate should proceed on the appropriations bill after the house had heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), so that hon. members might have such details as these two ministers were prepared to give with respect to the conditions and the proposals they had in mind in relation thereto. When I entered the house yesterday afternoon I had hoped-in fact I had understood-that that was the course we were to follow. With no information in the speech from the throne, such as is generally conveyed, it seemed that this was the method by which we could best have a debate on the second of those vitally important subjects.
There are other subjects that hon. members will wish to discuss and that undoubtedly will be brought up. Reports have appeared in the press, attributed to reliable sources in Ottawa, that the government intends to introduce some measures designed to deal with the inflationary pressures created by increased government spending, and by other circumstances which have arisen. The rapidly mounting cost of living and the very real threat of inflation are causing great concern today to all Canadians. Without some indication from the government whether it proposes to deal with this subject, and if so in what way, hon. members are not in a position to determine whether they should raise these questions in the debate at this time or should wait in the hope that proposals will be placed before the house to deal with them.
It was for that reason that I had hoped we might deal with the operative provision being introduced by the government in connection with the second of those two very important

subjects, just as we did with the first. When that had been dealt with, the government could then indicate what steps it proposed to take to deal with any of the situations arising as a result of the new expenditures and new taxation which may be approved by parliament.
It seemed to me that this would be a much more orderly and expeditious manner to deal with the questions before us. In view of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is to speak in this debate, I suggest to him that he consider the desirability of adjourning the debate after he and the leaders of the parties have spoken, and then proceed to deal with the appropriations bill-which is the operative measure under which we can most satisfactorily discuss the international situation and national defence- without dealing with other subjects about which we are still called upon to speculate, no matter how vitally important they may be, and thus diverting our attention from the second of the two main considerations which we were called together to discuss.
It is a terrible thing to realize that five years after the end of the second world war, at a time when we were all beginning to feel that we were returning to something in the nature of a normal life, we are confronted with the dreadful necessity of a vast rearmament program to meet the possible threat of an aggressor. Many people see in this urgent but unpalatable necessity the preliminary stages of a third world war. I have the strongest personal conviction that it can be the very opposite; that the military strength of the free nations may become the firm foundation of a longer period of peace during which the fundamental good sense of human beings everywhere may have time to create better understanding and mutual tolerance among the peoples of nations of widely divergent opinions, in a world which science and fast transportation have made too small for the kind of struggle we can already visualize.
In considering this subject, and in determining what we will do, it is necessary that we face with complete honesty the reality of the weaknesses of the free nations; that, with all the detachment of a surgeon handling his scalpel, we cut deep, remove any evidences of inefficiency, and restore to vigorous health all those organizations which will play their part in the common effort to preserve peace throughout the world.
Never in all history have the democracies been so outnumbered in trained men, weapons and machines of war as they are today. It is necessary that we face the actual arithmetic of that threat so that we may gauge the
The Address-Mr. Drew urgency and the necessity of dealing with the problem which is now before us.
The Russians have at least 175 fully mobilized divisions, of which at least one-third are armoured or mechanized. Russia has under its effective control also many more fully mobilized divisions in Poland under a Russian marshal; in Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Roumania, China, and, as we know only too well, in Korea. The ground strength of the axis power in 1939 as compared with that of the democracies was small in comparison with the Russian ground strength of today.
Let us then also examine the figures which have been made public at different times in recent weeks of the strength of the Russian army, navy and air force. The tank strength of these Russian divisions alone is estimated at 40,000. In numbers that is seven times the strength of the United States army, and nearly seven times the .estimated strength of the army of the United Kingdom. Just a short time ago the minister of defence in the United Kingdom estimated the Russian air strength at
19,000	military aircraft, including jet aircraft of the latest design, both fighters and bombers. It may well be that all these are not fully operational, although on the other hand reliable sources have given an even higher figure.
At sea the Russians are building up a large submarine fleet, with the help of the German technicians whom they have absorbed in eastern Germany. Reliable sources estimate the present submarine fleet at not less than 360, with possibly as high as 200 of them being long-range craft capable of high speed both on the surface and under water. It is estimated that some of those submarines are capable of twenty knots an hour, submerged, which would make it possible for them to roam over five times the area which could be covered by submarines of the last war.
These figures apply only to Russia, and do not include any of the satellite countries, some of which have tremendous armament plants. I am thinking of Skoda in Czechoslovakia, which was one of the largest, if not indeed the largest armament plant in Europe. Manning all these tanks, aircraft, submarines, weapons and machines of war are 2,800,000 men now under arms. It is estimated that with mobilization Russia could place between five and a half and six million men under arms within a few months, and raise their effective armed strength to something like 350 divisions.
I have recited these figures because I believe it is wise to place them in comparison with those of the free nations, only to
112	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Drew emphasize the reality that we must face in considering the problems before us. While our thoughts have been directed- so much toward Korea in these past few months, and while our thoughts will continue to be directed toward Korea and the outcome of events there, we must never divert our thoughts from the great cradle of freedom in our western civilization, where the real issues must perhaps be ultimately decided.
In western Europe today, against some eighty Russian divisions, there are not more than twelve divisions of all the nations of the western union. It is not a picture which should leave any of us with the thought that we can afford to accept anything but absolute certainty in regard to the things we are doing in Canada.
It is against that reality, which we, along with the other free nations, must recognize, that the Minister of National Defence yesterday gave us the easy assurances that he did. The impression he left was that all is well, that there is nothing to be done that is not now being done to prepare for the defence of our homeland and to share the common cause of freedom.
True, we are only a nation of fourteen million people. There is no thought that we stand alone at any time. But with our vast productive power and with the high character and qualities of our people we must prepare for our own defence and our share of the general responsibility for peace in a way which is related to these grim realities. Developments in Korea have emphasized the fact that it is forces in being, ready to be used immediately, which will deter the Russians from other communist aggression and do what it should be the highest purpose of free men anywhere to do-prevent, by every possible means that human skill and human ingenuity can devise, a general war.
When the house was in session last June there was wholehearted acceptance of the decision of the United Nations to deal collectively with the Korean- situation. That decision is not now and has not been in issue. In this general debate I propose to deal with the things which, it seems to me, require to be done to meet the situation which we accept, and the situation we are preparing to meet.
As was stated yesterday by the seconder of the address in reply (Mr. Bennett), events of the past few months have brought to an end the idea of the nuclear concept of a Canadian defence force. Canadians have also learned that we did not have forces in being which were capable of meeting our defence requirements. It is with this knowledge that we must assume responsibility not only for providing additional sums for national


defence, but also, and probably much more important, for ensuring that the money which is spent will be well spent on military organization and munitions suitable for the task we now face as a member of the United Nations, as a member of the North Atlantic security pact, and under our joint arrangements with the commonwealth and the United States. The whole international scene has changed greatly since we last met in June. A new appreciation of our place in the collective system built up by the free nations to stem the tide of communism in the Atlantic area and throughout the world has taken form.
Undoubtedly there had been too great reliance upon the devastating effect of the atom bomb. Now we know that the atom bomb alone is not enough, and that a new pattern of aggression has taken form against which it is not possible to employ this dreadful weapon. On the other hand it can be said with certainty that only the atom bomb is giving the free nations a breathing spell to build up that measure of military strength which can restore and maintain peace throughout the world. The emphasis placed by Russian propaganda upon the banning of the atom bomb is the best evidence that it is still an effective deterrent to Russian arms. One of the things most noticeable to me while in Europe in recent weeks was the extent to which communist propaganda is centring upon banning the atom bomb. Their propaganda is clever and subtle. In France, Italy and elsewhere in Europe, posters designed to affect the thinking of the people in each community emphasize in the simplest possible forms the threat of the atom bomb, and seek to create the impression that this is part of a plan of aggression by the United States against which the people should prepare themselves.
It would be most unwise for us or for people in the other free nations to ignore the fact of this clever, simple and constant propaganda. I recall one simple poster showing a mother carrying her dead baby from the ruins. All that was stated b.elow that harrowing picture was: "Do your part in banning the atom bomb and demanding that the American imperialists do not use it against us or anyone else'\ That, is the kind of propaganda that is being carried on, and among people who have lived through the horrors of two world wars it is not difficult to imagine that some of it is having effect. On the other hand there has been great encouragement in the evidence given by the United Nations that it was in fact an effective instrument to stand in the face of aggression. I am confident that in the end that faith in the United Nations and

the strength of the democracies will overcome the influence of propaganda of the kind to which I have referred.
All of this merely emphasizes that to some extent we are working on borrowed time. Time is of the very essence of peace. It is not only what we do; it is how fast we do it. No one can say how long we can wait for the atom bomb to deter an aggressor, but certain it is that it is better to risk doing too much than to find that we have done too little. On the other hand, as was pointed out yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs we must not burden ourselves to such an extent as to wreck our economy and give the communists one form of victory without direct contact of any kind.
The vital question before us, and the question we must ask ourselves now, is not merely how much we can do, but how quickly we can do it. What we need now are not just plans the completion of which Canada is capable, but the quickest and most effective plans for building up defence. What we must do now is to make use of the resources we possess in the shortest time possible; and in this we can learn from the communists. The pattern of communist logistics is something that has disturbed many of the people living in the free nations. Their armies move with much less in the way of supplies and equipment than our armies require. They have improvised more than we have felt it necessary to do. That applies not only to Russia but also to the forces of the satellite countries which have been engaged in military action, either in civil war or otherwise.
It seems to me that we must be ready to improvise to some extent and to build our forces with what we have now and with what is readily available. We have many trained units in this country; we have the equipment, and it seems that we must adjust our minds to the simplest means of effective employment of what we have, while at the same time making our longer plans as well.
On the other hand it seems that what we must do is to stop talking in percentages. So far as I know, percentages have never won any struggle. It is what we have, it is what we are doing, not what the percentage is of something else. The percentage of the national income, the percentage of the national budget, the percentage of what somebody else is doing, undoubtedly gives some information. It may mean a lot of money, but it does not tell us what we want to know. It is not so much a case of what we can afford to do as it is a case of what we can afford not to do. Free nations can still prevent war. We certainly must not miss the chance we have to prevent it. Time, I say, in all that
The Address-Mr. Drew we do is of the essence of peace. The question is not one of percentages; the question is whether we have what we need. There will be no second chance in our lifetime if we fail.
May I emphasize my belief that in carrying out our new tasks it is imperative that we make every cent in every dollar count. The people of Canada, when they learned to their amazement a short time ago something of what the 'state of our defence forces really was, were disturbed not only by the fact that they were inadequate, but also by the fact that we had spent so much to produce so little.
Let us remember that at no time has this government been restrained from spending what it has requested for the purposes of defence. No government of Canada has had such a free hand in time of peace to prepare whatever defences are necessary. No government of Canada has ever spent anything approaching the sum that this government has spent on defence in years of peace. Since the end of the last war, in the last five years, Canada has spent $1,500 million on defence. The people are asking themselves what has been done with that $1,500 million. It is the responsibility and duty of every hon. member to know what has been done and to make sure that we know a great deal more about the additional expenditures we are being asked to support than we have been permitted to know in the past.
The government has never been asked to stint itself. We have asked that tfle government submit the affairs of the Department of National Defence to examination by a special committee of this house so that not only the expenditures but the organization of our defence forces could be examined in a manner that is regarded as suitable and satisfactory in other great enterprises carried on by this government on behalf of the people of Canada. That is the reason why we have continued to press for a special committee of the house on national defence. If there had been such a committee, all hon. members would have known a great deal more about the real state of our defence forces than we knew up to the time the situation was more fully disclosed a few weeks ago. Now that we are going to be asked to approve greatly increased expenditures of money, in all earnestness I urge the Prime Minister to reconsider the views he has expressed in the past and assure us that he will agree to the appointment of a special committee on national defence.
So far as I can recall, the only reason previously advanced for not appointing such a committee when it has been requested is that it would be contrary to our- established

The Address-Mr. Drew parliamentary procedure, and would be placing in the hands of members of the house the responsibility of government. I have sought to point out on other occasions, and I point out again, that at Westminster, which we still have the habit of describing as the mother of parliaments, they have a subcommittee on defence which has authority to call people before it and to obtain information in regard to expenditures; and since it has authority to inquire into the purpose of expenditures, with that authority goes an opportunity to examine into the organization and other details which necessitate those financial requirements. Even that, however, has not fully satisfied the members of the British House of Commons. I should imagine that most hon. members here would regard Mr. Churchill as possessing parliamentary experience and appreciation of the needs of our parliamentary system at least equal to that possessed by the Minister of National Defence. I say that in no offensive manner at all, but merely to point out that Mr. Churchill has not the same views as to the dangers of committees of this kind that have been expressed so often in this house by the minister. As recently as July 26 Mr. Churchill was discussing the need for .greater information in regard to defence than they are able to obtain through the committee they now have, a committee such as we have been asking for here. In view of the fact that it has been said so often that this would introduce something of the United States method, I think it might be well to place before the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence the views on the United States method expressed in the House of Commons by Mr. Churchill on that occasion. In referring to these congressional committees he said:
These congressional committees, especially those of the House of Representatives, have enormous powers of obtaining information for their members. They can summon generals, admirals, air marshals and other experts before them subject only to the veto of the minister in charge of the department, very rarely exercised, and can examine them to any extent, either in public or in secret.
There is no doubt whatever that the American House of Representatives exercises its responsibilities towards its constituents in a far more vigilant and rigorous manner than anything we have adopted over here. We are a very ill-informed body on defence questions compared to them . . .
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the members of the British House of Commons, including Mr. Churchill, are a very ill-informed body, with the subcommittee on defence which they have, all I can say is that we are denied any information at all which would really make it possible for us to exercise the measure of informed judgment we should be able to

exercise in respect to one of the most important subjects with which we shall ever be called upon to deal.
That being so, in all earnestness I repeat my request that the Prime Minister assure us today that a special committee on defence will be appointed, so that at this critical hour this whole subject may be dealt with on a non-political basis. I am certain that if such a committee is appointed the Prime Minister and all members of this house will find that it will work in harmony and with the one purpose of creating the highest degree of efficiency that can be brought about in our defence organization with such expenditures as may be made available by the members of this parliament. Recognizing how little the members of this house have been permitted to learn-and most certainly the statement of the Minister of National Defence yesterday added nothing to our information-I would go further and suggest that this committee should meet immediately, and that instead of this special session proroguing it should adjourn and come back to hear a report by that special committee on national defence at the earliest possible day.
Another reason why such a committee should be permitted to exercise the fullest measure of supervision over expenditures now being made, and over the additional expenditures we shall be asked to approve, is that the rapidly mounting cost of living and the inflation taking place before our eyes are causing concern to all Canadians, not only in the daily problems of their home lives but in the way they are threatening the effectiveness of our defence effort. As the dollar decreases in actual value through inflation, and as the increasing cost of living places new pressure on our whole domestic economy, it is certain that with the dollars we have we become less capable of performing the great tasks that are before us. As was very properly said yesterday by both the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence, in the struggle in which we are engaged it is essential not only that we prepare to defend ourselves by military force, but also that we preserve the security of the home life and the confidence of the people in our democratic system, which is just as essential a part of the victory over communism as the actual restraint of military aggression.
The danger of this inflation became apparent the moment the government found it necessary to make great expenditures to meet new military demands and to acquire supplies of various kinds. Government spending added to ordinary spending is always bound

to create inflationary pressures. As new demands are made for government expenditure to meet the increasing gravity of the situation, those pressures will increase. Steps could have been taken by the government, within their powers, to meet in some degree those pressures which were created. Steps should have been taken. Steps certainly should be taken now.
One of the difficulties with which we are confronted at the moment in discussing those steps is that we have not had placed before us a statement as to what the government is or is not prepared to do. In fact, in answer to a question just before the orders of the day were called it was indicated that the Prime Minister was not yet ready to inform the house whether or not certain steps would be taken; and that applies to any of the many steps which might be taken in a situation of this kind. For that reason it undoubtedly will be more satisfactory to defer further discussion of this subject until we have that information. I do urge the Prime Minister to tell us this afternoon what plans the government has to deal with this situation, which will become more threatening as greater government expenditure increases the pressures which already exist.
We know there are great difficulties, and I assure the Prime Minister and the members of the government that we are anxious to co-operate in every way we can in meeting a situation which is going to affect the daily life of every Canadian for years to come. We shall be able to co-operate only to the extent that we can base our remarks upon an actual knowledge of what is contemplated. The protection of our economy is part and parcel of the struggle in which we are engaged here, and in which the other democracies are engaged as well. In this case the fullest information will, I am sure, find a ready response. I am certain that it will be the basis upon which we can close our ranks and present a united front in regard to those things which are of such concern in every Canadian home today.
The last thing that we Canadians can afford is war. War can be prevented. The atom bomb is giving us the breathing spell. The United States, with its enormous industrial resources, is not alone. We have industrial resources out of all proportion to our population, as compared with other nations throughout the world. The United Kingdom has great skill and tremendous industrial resources, as have the other countries with whom we are associated in this common purpose. With that breathing spell, the combined
The Address-Mr. Drew strength of the free nations can preserve the peace which is the first consideration of every Canadian. I have very great hope today; for the first time in our history we have seen the free nations of the world joined in giving a positive undertaking that collectively they will resist aggression anywhere against the nations with which they are associated. It may well be that if we in this country, with all the energy, all the ability and skill we possess, do what we can with the utmost speed, the dark clouds in which we are now enveloped will pass, to reveal the brightest days yet known to mankind.
It is my purpose to move an amendment so that there may be discussion of certain steps. I have already indicated that, with nothing more than a bare indication of the two steps, it is difficult to discuss much of the detail now. We shall have the appropriation bill, and with the indications in that bill we shall be able to discuss, under the various headings, the proposals that are made. It is my intention to reserve the discussion of those steps until then. There will undoubtedly be other measures, further information as to which will be extremely helpful if the Prime Minister will give it to the house today.
There was some discussion earlier about whether the house should sit at eleven o'clock in the morning, as well as at three and at eight. I feel sure, that every member here wants to complete the business of this session as quickly as possible in the interests of the people of Canada. But the longer the information about the things we shall be called upon to consider is delayed, the more difficult it will be to give adequate consideration to those matters if we sit practically the whole day. Under our parliamentary system it is extremely important that, when a completely new proposal is placed before the house, those associated in the different parties in this house have an opportunity of meeting and discussing it. It is for that reason, and in the interests of the expeditious completion of the business of this special session, that it will be helpful if we have the greatest detail at the earliest possible moment.
I have said that I have great hope. I believe that hope on my part was increased through some of the contacts I had within the past few weeks. The spirit of the people of Britain today is remarkably good. So is the spirit in France and in Italy. I believe that is true of the spirit of the people throughout the whole of western Europe, as a result of the evidence that has been given of firm collective action to deal with aggression. If we can cast our eyes beyond the

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent immediate future, then we can undertake our task with a high heart. I like to feel that the sentiments of those who now face the future were well expressed in the words of a poem written during the first world war by Owen Seaman. Many of you will remember these lines; to me they express the sentiment that each one of us could hold at this time:
Ye that have faith to look with fearless eyes Beyond the tragedy of a world at strife,
And trust that out of night and death shall rise The dawn of ampler life;
Rejoice, whatever anguish rend your heart,
That God has given you for a priceless dower,
To live in these great times and have your part In Freedom's crowning hour.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we may well be coming to freedom's crowning hour. It is with the idea of laying a foundation for that discussion which will call for an examination of our own affairs, under our democratic system, that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon):
That the following words be added to the address: "We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to provide adequately for the defence of Canada and have failed to take steps to deal with inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living."

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of this house I have listened with much interest to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). As a Canadian I have listened to it with pride as well, b'ecause of the high tone of the remarks which he has addressed to this assembly and because of the evident desire of the hon. gentleman that all Canadians, regardless of party, do take heart in this new situation which unites the free peoples of the world in standing together against aggression and for the preservation of all they hold dear.
I have just received the terms of the amendment which the hon. gentleman has seen fit to place before the house. The amendment raises a question which I think is important for the people of Canada. It is important for their representatives to consider it seriously and it is proper that they should make a decision upon it. The amendment states that His Excellency's advisers have failed to provide adequately for the defence of Canada and have failed to take steps to deal with inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living.
Those are matters which are of grave concern to the people of Canada; and were it true that His Excellency's advisers had failed in their duty in that respect, such pronouncement should be made against them and they should be dismissed from office. That no one can gainsay. But the question 
arises: have they or have they not failed in the respects mentioned in this amendment?
There is no doubt that when this new Korean situation arose there were not in Canada any forces in being ready to cope with it. That is something which we frankly admit, but we do not admit that it constitutes failure of His Excellency's advisers to provide adequately for the defence of Canada. In the London Times of recent date I read with some interest quite an accurate account of the developments in that respect. I was glad to note that in that account the people of the United Kingdom were toeing informed through that great newspaper that as early as 1946 the representatives of Canada in the general assembly of the United Nations had been urging that the provisions made in the San Francisco charter be implemented, and that we in Canada be informed of the part we would be expected to take in any united action by the United Nations to prevent or to put down aggression; and that, because of the attitude of one of the permanent members of the security council and because of the fact that the security council was the agency which, under the charter, had been given primary responsibility for the maintenance of peace, it was never possible to make that progress.
The report then goes on to say that, in that situation, plans were made by Canada with its neighbours to the south to prepare for' the immediate defence of the North American continent; that at the same time efforts were made to bring about a union of those free nations who would act together for their respective protection; and that under those plans there was organized in Canada a system whereby we had a competent, highly-trained, mobile, airborne force that was going to take its part in continental defence and a system whereby we were training large numbers of competent officers and organizing an establishment which could be rapidly expanded in the event of general war.
But the Korean situation presented a new and different situation to the members of the United Nations, and a fortuitous one; because had it not been for the walkout from the security council months before of the representative of one of the great powers, there could have been no effective action by the security council, when armed aggression took place in Korea. That member would certainly not have allowed the resolution adopted at that moment to pass, without the exercise of his nation's veto that has been so frequently exercised to frustrate international action. Had it not been for that circumstance and the splendid international leadership given by the United States of America to the freedom-loving nations of the organization, we would

not have had that which I hope' will be a demonstration that the freedom-loving nations, through and under the charter of the United Nations, are capable of acting together to prevent and to put down aggression and threats to peace.
I- was comforted by the optimistic prospects held out by the leader of the opposition. I hope and feel as he does that we may be not far from the dawn of an era of lasting peace. I read in a recent dispatch that a diplomat of great experience had said that the prospects of a decade of peace were brighter now than they had been at any time since the outbreak of this cold war. But some other had added: "provided we get through the next decade of months without war." I am inclined to think that there is a lot of truth in that reservation. The free nations of the world are now undergoing a test which may be a very vital one. And when they do-as I hope and feel confident that they will, within the next ten months-demonstrate that united action- by them can be effective to put down aggression, I think that we can look forward then, with the confident expectations implied in the. speech of the. leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), to a long period of absence of war, if not full peace, because there cannot be full peace for us when we are in the throes of a nerve-wracking cold war.
I am not going to attempt to gainsay anything that the leader of the opposition said about the fact that we are living on borrowed time. That is probably to be attributed to the knowledge of the possession of and the fear of the use of the atomic bomb. I think that all would agree with him that those who are now aggressors in Asia have developed a form of aggression designed to be effective under conditions where the question of use of the atomic bomb does not arise, and that that new situation must be met.
His Excellency's advisers have done what they thought it was proper to do, namely, recommended to parliament what they think it is proper to recommend, so that Canada may do its part in the United Nations, action of another form to prevent the success of that other form of aggression against their freedom and their institutions. It will be for the people, through their representatives in this house, to say whether they believe or do not believe that His Excellency's advisers have failed in that respect.
The situation, the background, was described in a manner yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr, Pearson) which I think impressed us all. For his colleagues in the cabinet it was not a new impression, because the information which he placed before the house yesterday
The Address-Mr. St. Laurent had been constantly, as circumstances developed, placed, before us as the background for the decisions and recommendations which we had to make.
We agree with the leader of the opposition that what is necessary at this time is not so much to determine how much we can do, but how quickly we can act effectively, and add effectively to the forces the United Nations will require to make the demonstration that this new form of aggression is not and cannbt succeed against them. For that reason His Excellency's advisers recommended that there be established as rapidly as could be done a special brigade, -not earmarked only for implementation of Canada's obligations as one of the United Nations, or as one of the North Atlantic treaty nations, but earmarked specially for service in that domain. Hon. members will have to decide whether or not we set about it vigorously enough, whether or not it was a proper measure to take at that time, and whether it is to be realized as quickly as circumstances make it possible to realize it.
Yesterday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) gave the figures of the enlistments that had been made by the young men of Canada for the organization and completion of that force. And if it is not proceeded with rapidly enough in the opinion of hon. members it will not be through any failure of response from the young men of Canada who are being called upon to serve with efficiency, devotion and heroism in that force.
The leader of the opposition says that Russia and its satellites improvise and that we must improvise and make the best and most expeditious use of the resources at our disposal. It will be for hon. members to say whether we are doing that. I recognize the obligation, I recognize the responsibility, but I feel confident that we will satisfy the people's representatives in this house that that responsibility has been and is being fully discharged.
Again the hon. member referred to the matter which he raised at the last session of parliament, namely, the establishment of a committee on national defence; and he referred to a recent speech made by Mr. Churchill, commenting upon the manner in which the committee of the house of representatives of the United States obtains information and exercises influence on defence policies in that country. I have great respect and great admiration for Mr. Churchill, but I think that we in Canada perhaps read more closely the United States' and our own newspapers, and I would be surprised if the Canadian people were very favourably impressed

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent with the reports of some of the sittings of the committees of the house of representatives of the United States. I think it would be shocking to Canadians if at any moment the Minister of National Defence appeared before one of our committees, looked around and said: "Well, are there no spies from the Department of External Affairs in this committee to spy out what I am going to say?" I do not want to be critical of the system of any friendly nation. But I would say that the members of the government of Canada constitute what is in essence a defence committee of this House of Commons, and that each of them realizes his responsibility as a member of that committee. I feel that when the members of that committee have formulated recommendations, there is no reason to exclude from the consideration and examination of those representations any hon. member of this house. That is our system. We bring the recommendations here. All hon. members of the house are members of the committee that exists to represent the Canadian people, to scrutinize those recommendations and to make sure, each one taking his own individual responsibility, that they constitute the proper way of discharging the obligations of the parliament of Canada to the people of Canada.
The hon. member has said that since June the situation has changed-and it has changed. In June last, and prior to that time, the question before the house was whether the general policy being followed by the Department of National Defence to set up the organization that would be the best possible organization to carry out our share in the territorial defence of the North American continent, either on land, in the air or on the sea, was the proper organization to have, and whether we were or were not, as rapidly as circumstances permitted, doing our share toward the joint armament of the North Atlantic treaty nations so as to be in a position to resist, together, any aggression against any one of them.
At the present time a new situation has developed. As a consequence of this unexpected situation, it gives an opportunity to the United Nations as such to make together and within the terms of the charter a demonstration of their willingness and of their capacity to make the charter work in that respect, and to put down local aggression and remove threats to peace. That was something which none of the members of the United Nations had anticipated.
It so happened that there were in the immediate vicinity land forces of the United States of America. They were there because of the obligation they had accepted at the


cessation of hostilities against Japan. They were the only ground troops available to render immediate assistance to the arms of the South Koreans themselves, and they have done it in such a magnificent and heroic manner that it makes it, I think, all the more encouraging for other members of the United Nations to follow under their leadership.
All the other nations were in a situation similar to our own. It so happened that the United Kingdom had troops in Hong Kong, which were there for another purpose, and which within the last few days are being added to the forces of the United States and will be replaced in Hong Kong by troops to be brought from elsewhere.
There may be some little difference in the time required for each nation to put itself in a position to meet an unexpected and unforeseen situation. Members of parliament will have it as their responsibility to say if the time we are taking is longer than it should be. If that is their conclusion they will be obliged, by their responsibilities to their constituents, to say so by their votes.
I do not think they will find that that is the situation at all, and I do not think they will be able to agree with the suggestion in the amendment, that His Excellency's advisers have failed to provide adequately for the defence of Canada.
Prices have been going up. Prices have been going up all over the world. I do not think there is any country in the world which has not had a greater degree of inflation than this portion of the North American continent, from the gulf of Mexico to the North pole. But there has been inflation here as well as elsewhere. It was asserted to me, in a conversation which was designed to give me the kind of advice that one having the responsibilities of the office I occupy should get, that of course no nation could expect to get away with a lesser degree of inflation than that which might develop in the United States, but that it was extremely important to do all that should be done and to avoid anything that should be avoided to the end that our inflation might not be greater than that which took place south of the border. So far it has not outrun anything that has taken place south of the border.
It might. It would be disastrous if it did. It would be calamitous if it did; and we certainly must do everything within the ingenuity of man to prevent it. The pressures are not going to be substantially increased by the expenditures now contemplated. We must realize that the amount of capital investment going on in our country is of the order of several	billions-several	billions being

expended each year for the improvement of plants and permanent services required for the development of the resources of this young nation. And what is going to be required for armament for ourselves or for our neighbours has got to come out of our production. Our production will either have to be increased or it will have to be diverted to the degree that a portion of it will be required for the purposes of armament.
But in any event it could not be of the order of ten per cent of what is now being used for capital development; and the pressures that could result from, the diversion of something less than ten per cent from that which goes into capital development would not, I feel confident, add anything substantial to the other pressures on prices of commodities and services.
Nevertheless that is a matter which the representatives of the people must carefully examine. If they come to the conclusion that we have failed or are failing to do anything which would be of substantial benefit to prevent further inflation or greater increases in the cost of living, it will be their responsibility to agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I am confident that they will not come to any such conclusion.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) asked if I could not at this time give some further information about the government's plans. I shall not be able to give positive information but I can give some negative information. I can say to the house at this time that we are not planning at this session to ask parliament for any enabling legislation which would empower us to impose a general system of controls on wages and prices. That we are not proposing to do at this time. That is something which normally is in the field of provincial jurisdiction. We have not convinced ourselves that in a general way the situation is such as to justify us to attempt to displace provincial jurisdiction in those regards.
There are certain other measures which the Department of Justice has been considering, and I think that that consideration is just about completed, as to whether, without any general invasion of the jurisdiction given by the constitution to the provinces, some measures of an anti-inflationary character could be justified. Just as soon as the matter can be completed, and it may be within hours or within days, it will be announced and parliament will have to say whether we have been diligent, whether we have proceeded with the required diligence to meet the situation.
We have heard reproaches such as those that are contained or implied in this motion.
The Address-Mr. St. Laurent On a great many occasions we have had to meet the charge of not fulfilling properly our responsibilities to the Canadian people. When that question has been put to the Canadian people it has been considered carefully and the answer is now reflected by those who have come here to represent them in the House of Commons. The present situation is very much the same, although it might appear to be more critical than it has been at times in the past. The conduct of His Excellency's advisers will have to be judged by the same rigorous standards and I feel confident that it will receive the same measure of approval that it has received in the past.
