It is not intended at this time to ask parliament to enact any repressive measures directed against those misguided and, I am glad to say, rather few communists that we have in Canada. We still believe that it is better to meet them and fight them above ground than it is to have them burrow underground.
I am sure that the leader of the opposition is sincere in his desire to co-operate and I welcome that assurance. I feel, as he does, that the situation will require the greatest efforts that all good Canadians can put forth. We must all do our part so that we may have in this country that confident feeling which he found in the United Kingdom, in France and in Italy and so that there may persist among the peoples of all the free nations the impression that at last there is something of an international character that is working and that will work and that will assure to us all those prospects which the leader of the opposition so eloquently delineated in his address.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with all those who have already congratulated the mover and seconder of the address. I was happy indeed to hear the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett) make his maiden speech yesterday and I congratulate him upon the manner of its delivery as well as upon its subject matter. The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) has spoken in the house on several occasions but he certainly enhanced his reputation as a speaker and parliamentarian when he spoke yesterday.

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
I am sorry that we are having a debate on the address of the description we are having at the present time. It is rather difficult to deal with many of the problems that need to be discussed at this time in a debate which was introduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minis' ter of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I think that fact has tended to narrow the scope of our discussions in a manner which is rather regrettable. However, as time goes on we may find that the debate has been enlarged considerably and it may be that, contrary to the government's expectation, the adjournment or prorogation of the house will be delayed. I hope that that will not occur.
I listened with a great deal of interest yesterday to the speeches of the minister of external affairs and the Minister of National Defence. I was particularly interested in what the minister of external affairs had to say regarding the international situation. I am sure that there is no difference of opinion as to the gravity of the international situation or as to Canada's determination to play her part as a member of the United Nations in preventing aggression and removing the dangers of war, we hope permanently in the future.
As I sat here this afternoon I looked back over the years since I have been here, the years that led up to 1938 when there was aggression by the Japanese in Manchuria, aggression by Mussolini against the Ethiopians and the situation which developed in Spain with the intervention of the dictatorships of Germany and Italy and eventually intervention also on the part of the Soviet union. All these events culminated with the Munich agreement.
I felt that if perchance the league of nations had been organized as the United Nations is organized today the aggression might have been stopped at one or other of those early points and the terrible war which came upon us in 1939 prevented. I say, "might have been" advisedly because no one can tell what might have happened. May I say that throughout all those years I believed that the league of nations should have had a police force behind it to enforce international decisions for the maintenance of peace. However throughout those years I shared with many people a growing disillusionment as it appeared that the term "collective security" was nothing but a catch phrase, and that we could not rely either upon the statesmanship of the leaders of the great democratic nations or indeed upon the one instrument we had built up over those years and that failed us so badly. Perhaps I should not say the league 
of nations failed us so badly, because after all it was the statesmen of the world who failed the great ideal which lay behind the league of nations.
Now we have set up another world organization. I had the great privilege of seeing the birth of the United Nations at San Francisco. I shared with the delegates of at least all the democratic nations present the idea that we were building a foundation which in time would provide the peoples of the world with a structure under which they might find shelter and eventually universal peace. But here we are, only five years later, engaged as a country not in a war in the usual sense but at least preparing to take part in police action in Asia in order to drive back those who have acted as aggressors against a nation recognized and indeed established by the United Nations Organization.
I think we would be well advised to remember that perhaps the most striking statement on this situation was made, not by a European statesman but by the leader of a great Asiatic people, Pandit Nehru of India. I believe we should keep that statement not only before ourselves but before the public. In the mail this morning I received eleven letters, I think signed by people who had gathered together, though of that I am not sure, sent by special delivery and urging me to support Pandit Nehru. Well, in what we have done up to the present time I believe we have supported the statement on the Korean situation by Pandit Nehru. I am not going to quote from any newspaper, capitalist, socialist or otherwise.
I am going to quote the official India information service, circulated by the high commissioner of India from 121 Slater street in this city. This is a special release on the conference granted to the press of India by Pandit Nehru who had this to say on the Korean situation:
When North Korea launched the invasion on South Korea it became evident from all information available that this was a large-scale, well-planned invasion. The border conflicts between the two countries as well as the internal conflicts had a bearing on the situation. But they were dominated by this major fact of a well-planned invasion and aggression on South Korea. In the delicate and precarious balance existing in the world, any such invasion and aggression was fraught with the most dangerous possibilities. If aggression was allowed to proceed and to succeed then the structure of the United Nations would have inevitably collapsed and a large scale war would have resulted. The whole basis of the United Nations is to bring about settlement of international disputes by peaceful means. If aggression takes place and the aggressor ignores the United Nations completely then only two choices are left:	Either the United Nations should
condemn that aggression and try to put an end to it or it should come to the conclusion that it has ceased to be an effective instrument of peace and leave the decision of any dispute to war.
Thus in the context of events the security council had no alternative but to declare North Korea as

aggressor and subsequently call upon the members of the United Nations to meet this armed attack and restore international peace. Whatever justification might be advanced for this aggression, and whatever might have preceded it, may have some importance, but it does not take away from the fact of a well-planned aggression.
Throughout the world I am sure there is a universal desire for peace, shared by the peoples of Asia, Europe and indeed of all continents. The world cries aloud for peace. What we could do if instead of having to divert millions and indeed billions of dollars to preparations for defence and perhaps ultimately expenditures on war! We could utilize these vast resources to build up a world society in which all men could look forward to decent standards of living and measures of security. Yet I suppose that never in the history of our time has the world felt more insecure than at present. A few moments ago the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) referred to the atomic bomb. I have no doubt that people throughout the world fear that one day this fell weapon may be used again to blot out large portions of the population of some countries. Let me say once more that we believe atomic energy should be completely under international control, and that, under the United Nations, provision should be made for adequate, constant and unrestricted inspection of all plants producing fissionable material. Of course that is where we disagree with the Soviet union, which will not agree to a comprehensive system of inspection but, on the contrary, is prepared to agree to inspection only to a limited and inadequate extent.
We believe we must continue to support collective security because Canada is a small nation, with a population of fourteen million people inhabiting the northern half of a great continent. We cannot hope to remain at peace if we rely only upon ourselves for defence, so we must participate in measures of collective security to the fullest extent of our power and resources. I think, however, we can offer a criticism of the government on the manner in which it handled the Korean situation. If we look over the record we find that on July 12 Dean Acheson stated to the world that offers of ground troops would be very helpful. Two days later the Secretary General of the United Nations telegraphed all the member countries an urgent appeal for ground troops to assist in putting the aggressors in Korea back beyond the 38th parallel. Six nations did reply immediately. They were members, in part, of the commonwealth of nations with which we are associated: Australia, the United Kingdom, New Zealand. In addition, there were Turkey, Bolivia and Thailand.
The Address-Mr. Coldwell
The point I am making in criticism of the government is that when that occurred I thought and I said that parliament should have been called immediately to make provision for our participation in assisting the United Nations forces in driving back the aggressor in Korea. It was not until August 7, almost a month after the first call, that the Prime Minister announced that a special United Nations brigade would be recruited and that parliament would meet in the course of the next six or seven weeks which would have brought us to the end of September. Parliament, because of another grave matter, met in the meantime, and we can now discuss the problem of assistance to the United Nations as well as the problem of our own defence.
I am certain that the vast majority of the Canadian people are ready and willing to assist the United Nations in bringing a speedy end to the aggression in Korea. May I add that I believe the bringing of this aggression to a speedy end is of vital importance to the whole world. If there is a prolonged fight in Korea I fear the United Nations Organization may lose the confidence of some of the smaller nations who may think of their own country being subjected to aggression, and only after devastation and a prolonged fight restored to independence and peace. Consequently I am of the opinion that the sooner effective help can be given to the United Nations forces in the present circumstances, the better it will be for the peace of the world and for the United Nations Organization.
The international crisis created by aggression in Korea enabled the people of Canada to show a large measure of unity. I believe that all parties in this house are now pledged to support the principle of collective action, collective security, and all that is implied in those terms. So far as we are concerned, as we said at the time, we welcome the prompt action of the security council in connection with this matter. We believe that the police action necessary must not be left to one nation, or even mainly to one nation. The danger is very great that if the whole campaign is dominated by, we will say, the United States, it does give an opportunity to the communist propagandists to present this police action to the nations of the world, and particularly to the nations of Asia, as American imperialism. Of course that statement is absurd on the face of it because of the manner in which the present situation arose, and the manner in which all the non-communist nations of the world have co-operated in supporting police action to stop the aggression. Nonetheless the active parti-

The Address-Mr. Coldwell cipation of many nations is necessary in order to demonstrate to the people of the world, and to the people of Asia, that this is not an American engagement, but is indeed a United Nations police action supported by members of the United Nations everywhere and strictly in accordance with the provisions of the United Nations charter.
May I suggest to the government that once again we should do what Canada did at the United Nations assembly in 1946 when the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) led our delegation, of which I had the honour of being a member, namely, to demand that the military staffs of the great powers, as provided by the charter, should meet to fulfil the intention of the charter, and to bring about a real collective security force for the security council. I know it may be said immediately, "but Russia is one of the five great powers; there would be difficulties in that respect". That is true. I do not know how long the other nations of the world can continue to allow the will of the vast majority of nations to be thwarted by one nation. If it is impossible to gather together the general staffs of all the great powers on the security council then the general staffs of the powers that will join together for real collective security should be called to meet.
May I say then that the goal in Korea at the moment is the defeat of the aggressor. But that should not be the ultimate goal. The ultimate goal of the United Nations is to promote in Korea the emergence of a free, democratic and united nation. This means doing something we have failed to do hitherto. I am not going to quote from articles that have been written by men who have no sympathy for communist ideas, and which have appeared in reputable papers such as the Manchester Guardian. One of the things we have failed to do, both in Korea and elsewhere in Asia-I think the minister of external affairs implied this clearly yesterday-is to devise a policy that will win the support of the peasants and workers; the people who have been exploited and are still being exploited by the governments of those backward countries. I think that, unfortunately, we have not yet placed the economic and social aims of the United Nations action in Korea in the manner in which those aims should have been formulated and placed before the world.
Two or three weeks ago I listened one evening to a broadcast, which was a rebroadcast over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stations from the Mutual Broadcasting system of the United States, in which a number of so-called experts on this side of the Pacific ocean spoke to various war correspondents in Japan. I listened with a great deal of interest to a Canadian voice because

it was a good one, that of Mr. J. B. McGeachy, speaking from Toronto. The question that he asked several times was this:	What are the
war aims in Korea? What are you telling the people of Korea? The only reply he could get was that we were aiming to achieve certain military objectives. I knew, of course, that that was not what Mr. McGeachy was really asking. Unless we can say to the people of these Asiatic countries that we are going to deliver them from the oppression of the land owner, that the peasant is going to get the land so that he can make a living on it and be secure on it; that the coolie is not going to be exploited by the industrialist; or that the ordinary common man in those countries is not going to be oppressed by war lords and by other people of that type, we are not going to be successful in winning ultimately the victory over communist propaganda and communist aggression in Asiatic countries.
I deplore the fact that we have failed to place before the Asiatic peoples the promise *-and not only the promise but something in a material way to show that we mean that promise-to improve their position. We have said-and I repeat it this afternoon-that we believe that the only secure basis for peace in the world can be found in economic planning of the world's resources. That does not mean planning under one great authority, but on a regional basis and in a manner that will enable all the people of the world to develop their resources and to enjoy a better standard of living. Effective assistance to raise the living standards everywhere and a real program to increase the productivity of nations backward in technological experience, in mechanization and so on, in Asia, Africa, South America and elsewhere is the only way in which we shall achieve permanent peace in the world. It is no good to say that our aim is to contain communism or to prevent its spread unless we do something really effective to prevent that spread. The hungry peoples of the world are not interested in democratic ideals or in democratic systems of government and all the rest of it; but they are interested in food and in economic progress. I therefore say that the purpose of our country, and of other countries like this one, should be to devise ways and means of providing them with the means to progress, not only because it is our moral duty to do so but because it is to our self-interest to put it on the lowest possible level.
We have, of course, watched what has happened over the years, and I am not wholly critical because some good things have been done. Important steps have been taken in that direction. We have the success of the Marshall plan in rebuilding the European economy; the recent decision of the

Atlantic pact nations to increase their economic co-operation, and I hope that that decision will be put into effect; the adherence of the United States and Canada to the organization for European co-operation; the international wheat agreement; and the work generally of the economic commission of the United Nations. These are all good examples of international co-operation-among the western democratic powers, I should add- and on a scale that the world has never before seen.
All I am saying is that we must continue that kind of thing and must do much more than we have already done. I am afraid that we have been somewhat content to pay lip service to these matters without giving sufficient reality to them. Even yesterday, when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), in that excellent address he gave to the house, was speaking along those very lines, I thought: We have heard the same thing so often from the government and from ministers of external affairs, that this is what we should do. But when we look at our present proposals, what are they as far as we can get them from the government today? To do all that we can to defeat the aggression in Korea; to spend another $150 million on defence; and if I understood the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) aright yesterday, in his illuminating address, all I can say is that we are going to spend perhaps several hundred millions of dollars in the provision of armaments for the western European countries. Probably that is all very necessary. But what are we going to do to help to raise the standards of living of the depressed peoples of the world in order that we may defeat communist propaganda which can flourish only where there is poverty, misery and want? That is the point that always strikes me. We do all these other things. We are prepared to spend millions and millions of dollars on armaments and so on, and we must spend them. But what comparable action are we going to take in order to do the essential things that everybody tells us must be done, namely to assist as rapidly as we can in feeding and in raising the standards of living among the depressed peoples of Asia?
I listened to Dr. Kagawa, the great Japanese Christian who has played so important a part since the war in encouraging democratic organizations in Japan and who was a member of the government of Japan for some time since the war. What I have just said was the message that he gave to the Christian churches of Canada when he was here three or four weeks ago. In effect he said that if the western nations had done for the peasants
The Address-Mr. Caldwell of southern Korea what they might have done and should have done-and incidentally what he said they did in Japan with regard to land-we would have had support from the peasants of Korea and perchance would not have been in the great difficulty we are in with regard to this war today. I therefore say that we must consider more than the military aspects of the present situation. I know that point has been emphasized by a good many people but we must heed and make that emphasis as a nation.
I have a few quotations, one or two of which are worth putting on the record; I cannot put them all on. I notice that Herbert Morrison, lord president of the council in the United Kingdom, speaking at Manchester a few days after this aggression occurred, on July 2, 1950, said this:
While armed opposition is necessary in reply to armed aggression, the path we and other like-thinking people must follow is in removing the causes of communism, by alleviating the malnutrition and misery that affects so many millions of people, particularly throughout Asia.
And then the other day, at the conference at Lake Couchiching in this province, the secretary to the Indian High Commissioner in Canada, Mr. Banerjee, said this:
What is wanted is immediate action on a war basis in overcoming the poverty of Asia. In Korea the United Nations did not hesitate to take immediate action against the aggression. Similar immediate action on a war footing should be taken against poverty, disease, illiteracy.
Note the emphasis "on a war footing".
At the Colombo conference that my hon. friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), attended, the official communique of January 14, 1950, said much the same thing. The communique read as follows:
It was recognized that, in the changing conditions brought about by recent developments in this area, progress depends mainly on the improvement of economic conditions. The conference was impressed by the magnitude of the contribution which the success of progressive policies in this area could make to the peace and prosperity of the world.
We give lip service to such fine sentiments, but we do very little beyond that.
However, I want to refer to some other matters, and I must do so briefly because my time is rapidly running out. First, in regard to our own defence situation, once again I am going to put before the house what we have so often said, and what indeed other hon. members in other parties have said from time to time, but which incidentally their parties when in power have not carried out. We are alarmed at the profiteering in the production of munitions of war. In the last session we did condemn the removal of the 5 per cent profit limit on the production or sale of war

The Address-Mr. Coldwell supplies in this country in connection with our present defence program. Since we are going to spend $150 million more on our defence and several hundred millions in the provision of supplies for western Europe, we believe at this session we should consider the nationalization of the production-not necessarily the industry at this present session- and the sale of armaments and munitions. We certainly should re-impose the excess profits tax to deal both with the excess profits that may be made in war industry or out of the present inflationary situation, I might add; and may I also say that I believe the time has long since passed when a tax should be imposed on an undue increase in the value of capital assets. Moreover, we need action to stop the rising cost of living. We believe that that can only be done by re-introduction of beneficial price controls and necessary subsidies on at least the necessities of life.
May I say how thoroughly I agreed with the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he said that there must be no halt to our own social progress. If we wish to get the Canadian people behind the great effort for defence, and in the event of war behind the great war effort that this country might have to make, then there must be no diminution in the social services already established. Moreover, the promise implied in the recommendations, for example, of the old age pension committee of last June should be carried out in spite of the expenditures we must face in connection with our rearmament program.
In order to get our view more completely before the house, Mr. Speaker, I am going to move a subamendment to the amendment made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). The amendment of the leader of the opposition reads in this way:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to provide adequately for the defence of Canada and have failed to take steps to deal with inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living.
We wish to add the following words:
By the imposition of price controls and the provision of necessary subsidies; we regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to include in Canada's defence program substantial economic aid for underdeveloped countries, for it is the opinion of this house that the spread of communism cannot be prevented by military action alone, but only by the provision, in addition, of all possible assistance to bring about social and economic progress in such countries.
An economic policy to meet the needs of the Canadian people at this time is essential. We have seen the prices of basic foods rise in a spectacular manner. The Prime Minister says that after all we live beside the United States and that our level of inflation has not gone


beyond the level of inflation in the United States, so he proposes to do nothing about it now. But I want to point out that until we made the over-hasty withdrawal of beneficial controls and subsidies our price level in this country was very much lower than the price level in the United States. Now we see it not only catching up but being in danger in some respects even of passing beyond the price level that the United States inflation has brought about in that country.
In the last day or so in this city the price of a loaf of bread has been increased by one cent. The cost of milk increased by one cent a quart this morning. I am not saying that the farmers do not need the extra cent a quart for their milk, but I am saying that the greatly increased cost of production that the farmers have to bear is reflected in the prices that the consumers have to pay; and that if we had beneficial controls, or if we had the kind of subsidy we had on commodities of this description during the war, we could retain a price level that would enable mothers of families to purchase supplies of food that are essential to the future welfare of this country, because the children of the nation are the greatest and best assets that we have. Therefore I am pointing this out. We need the continuance of rent control, particularly in a city such as Ottawa where we have people coming in on account of our defence program. I know of young army officers-in fact I lived near one until a few days ago at a summer cottage. He does not know now, after waiting all summer, where he will put his wife and family in the coming winter months. He cannot buy a house, not I presume because of inflated prices but because of the very nature of his work. He does not know how long he will be posted to the city of Ottawa. There are many others in the same circumstances in this city and elsewhere at this time.
We need effective action to halt price-fixing and other restrictive practices by monopolies and combines. A few days ago we were discussing a strike in the house, and we were complaining because the men were seeking an increase in wages. They had fulfilled every part of our law in doing it, and finally they came to the regrettable decision, regrettable to all of us, no matter what were our points of view on the strike, and a strike occurred. But before they came to that conclusion they had to take certain legal steps. It seems to me the time has come when we should not allow any monopoly or industry to set prices without having to show, if called upon, that the prices they set are fair and reasonable. For example, we see the prices of tires taking two jumps in a few days; yet
12b

we are told that the Polymer plant has plenty of rubber available, and we know that rubber is still coming in from the Malay peninsula.
I say that to prevent regrettable strikes such as the one we had lately, there should be consultation with trade union representatives to devise an over-all wage program which will permit more effective action in holding the price line, while assuring workers a fair and adequate standard of living and income. We did that pretty effectively during the war; why can we not attempt to do something of the kind now?
I have had to deal briefly with these matters at the conclusion of my address so as to bring them before the house, although I had wanted to elaborate to a greater extent than I have been able to do. After all our attention has been taken with the war situation in Korea. May I say before I take my seat how pleased I was yesterday when the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in discussing the Korean situation, made it abundantly clear that Canada was participating in the United Nations action in Korea, and that we were in no way involved in the Formosan situation. I said some time ago, and I now repeat, that the only thing to do-and it should have been done long ago-is to say to Chiang Kai-shek, "Get out of Formosa and stay out of Formosa", so as ultimately to give the Formosan people an opportunity to choose their own form of government

because they were once a free and independent people, and not so many decades ago at that.
I cannot go into that phase of the matter further except to say that the minister has the support at least of this group in the house in the attitude he has expressed from time to time in connection with Formosa, and the difficulties that have arisen in connection with it.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I have put before the house today not only my own opinions but, since we have just held a national convention, the considered opinions of the movement for which at this moment I have the honour to be spokesman in this debate.

speechtext:
At the outset of my remarks may I offer the traditional compliments to the mover and seconder on their most excellent addresses delivered in the house yesterday. Both these young men gave promise in their speeches, and I would compliment specially the hon. member who seconded the address, because this was his maiden speech.
The speeches yesterday of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) indicated plainly that in the days ahead Canada faces perhaps the most serious situation in her history. It is true that this country is not at war with any other country, but as a nation we are committed to whatever action the United Nations has decreed should be taken. Such action would be taken collectively with all other signatory nations of the San Francisco charter, and taken as a result of the fact that we hold membership in the United Nations. We are committed to take action collectively with all other signatory nations to put down aggression in Korea or wherever it may occur.
At this point we do compliment the United States on the prompt action they took immediately after the aggression of the Northern Koreans. If we are to play our full part as a nation there must obviously be a maximum level of Canadian unity. Unfortunately however there are in Canada today some grievances which seriously affect that unity. During two or three weeks of the summer I had an opportunity to travel through western Canada and to talk with many people. I found that there were certain paramount problems about which they complained, and the first of these was the freight rates situation.
The people in the west definitely feel that the government has not taken the action that should have been taken to remove the grievous disability from which they suffer in the matter of freight rates. There is discrimination in favour of the east. They know that, and they are not satisfied. They will not be satisfied until that discrimination is removed, because it puts them in a desperate position. They simply cannot compete with others in Canada under the existing freight rates structure. I say the government must take action as soon as possible to remove that grievance, if they are to expect Canadian unity to meet trials and difficulties in the days ahead.
The second grievance, which I shall discuss only briefly, is that of the cost of living and of prices. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that there

The Address-Mr. Low is every evidence that profiteering is going on in many lines today. I do not suggest that that profiteering is on the part of the small retailer; I do not believe it is. But I do think there is room for investigation to see just who is profiteering.
I suggest that the government should take immediate steps to institute such an investigation, and to put a stop to any practice of this kind. We hope the government's program to meet a condition of inflated prices and an increased cost of living is not going to be confined solely to high taxation. One would gather that that may be so, from what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said this afternoon. But the cost of living must be tackled, and tackled seriously, and with effective remedies. There is a remedy at hand. We have already suggested what our views would be in the matter. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that the effective remedy is to put on overall controls. I do not think we need to do that at this time; but I do suggest seriously and earnestly that we introduce a system of subsidies on certain selected items in the cos't of living, and see to it that consumer prices are kept down, without having any ill effect upon the producers of those goods.
Certainly the government is in a position to take some action in the matter of hidden taxation that inevitably pushes up the cost of living and purchase prices to a point where our people are placed in an almost impossible position. I hope that when the government brings in its taxation measure it will have considered well this whole problem of the cost of living and that the tax measure which we understand will be coming in will not impose upon the Canadian people a tax that will spiral costs or push up the cost of living.
In the splendid speech that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made yesterday, I think perhaps the best I have heard him make, he declared that it is of importance for us to understand our enemy. He then outlined in some detail the main features of soviet communist imperialism. In the course of this explanation the minister of external affairs stated that we must expect attacks by this insidious foe of free humanity in any part of the globe. I agree, and every one of us here must agree, that it is important for us to know our enemy. We should be thoroughly familiar with every possible detail concerning him and his aims.
It has occurred to me since yesterday afternoon that it is also important for us to understand how Russian communist imperialists have become our enemies. It seemed to me that it would be most useful if we could


determine exactly by what process Russia has become so powerful and so belligerent between 1917 and the present time. Here is a nation which at the turn of the century was a push-over for the comparatively weak Japan. Here is a country that in 1914-17 was considered to be a good-natured, plodding conglomeration of racial groups with no fixed intentions and certainly with no threatening abilities.
How could this amazing transformation occur in a period of about thirty years? Was Russia's rise to the position of being the foremost belligerent in the world the result of accidental growth or was it the result of a definite policy on the part of powerful interests inside as well as outside Russia? Perhaps the facts which I shall now present may help to clarify, at least to some extent, the whole question and provide some answer to it.
The. question certainly must be not just who is our enemy. Certainly it is not the Koreans. I think the Koreans are being used as tools and they are going to have visited upon them terrible things as a result of what they have allowed themselves to become. In a book written by Mr. George Lansbury, former chairman of the British Labour party, entitled, "Looking Backwards and Forwards", published in 1935, is to be found a detailed exposition of the manner in which Lenin and Trotsky were financed as far back as 1907 by a group of Wall street bankers. It transpires that these bankers were former German nationals who got out of Germany and established themselves in Wall street, New York. All of this is admitted by Trotsky himself in his history of the Russian revolution.
In 1915 Paul Rodzianko quoted the president of the Russian duma as saying:
Some people are In favour of peace, but they dare not speak. Rasputin will not work for peace for he is run by a ring of banks who make money out of the war.
Could this possibly be the Dresdner bank and banking group brought together by Jacob Schiff and Paul Warburg in New York. * There is pretty authentic evidence available to show that this same ring did finance the Japanese in the war against Russia earlier in the 1900's.
Possibly the most monumental piece of evidence that the international group which I mentioned financed the Russian revolution was the report of the French high commissioner in the United States early in 1919, from material supplied by the United States secret service. The report brought forward indisputable evidence that the firm of Kuhn,

Loeb and Company of Wall street had fomented and financed the Russian revolution. Furthermore, it declared that the same group had the contracts for the industrialization of Russia beforehand. Evidently the Krupps, the general dyes trust, the Hugo Stinnes and other concerns, directed or owned plants in Russia, most of them financed by the international, group amongst which was the Dresdner bank. Much of the capital had been smuggled out of Germany to Switzerland during a time when Germany claimed she was too poor to pay reparations. It is estimated that from 19 to 30 billion marks at the rate of 15 to the dollar were smuggled out during that time and went into war and industrial plants in Holland, Russia and Switzerland.
A report which appeared in the New York Times of March 24, 1917, seems to me more than sufficient to indicate that the Wall street group of international banks were interested in the Russian revolution. George Kennan reported at a meeting that day that Mr. Jacob Schiff had heavily financed revolutionary propaganda amongst 50,000 Russian prisoners of war in Japan, as far back as 1905. It is significant to note that this New York meeting was held in celebration of the outbreak of the Russian revolution, and at it a message was read from Mr. Schiff expressing his pleasure at the achievement of "What we had hoped and struggled for these long years." I imagine it is something of a shock to many people that a man from the most powerful banking house in the world should express his satisfaction in such a manner at the outbreak of the Russian revolution.
If further evidence is needed that this international banking group financed the revolution it is to be found in documents seized from the bolsheviks by the Kerensky government, and later established by the Sisson report in the United States. These documents named Warburg's bank as providing large funds for munitions for Trotsky. A close study of official Russian statements over the past 20 years indicates one policy which has not wavered. That policy is to use war to further the plan for world revolution.
Away back on November 26, 1920, Lenin proclaimed this:
Our salvation would be more readily assured if the imperialist powers became embroiled in a war.
On February 21, 1935, the political bureau of the communist international, after being addressed by Stalin, passed a resolution in which it said:
The political bureau is definitely convinced that a new world war is absolutely inevitable, but explains this as the obvious preparation for the world revolution. With the aim of self-preservation,
The Address-Mr. Low
and in the interests of the world revolutionary movement, the soviet government must do all possible to enter the camp of the states which build the strongest coalition.
One of the most remarkable pieces of evidence of Russian policy will be found outlined in the book "La Greve est un Combat" by Lozovsky, who was later appointed head of the Moscow foreign office, where he became the political adviser to Molotov. His chief aim in life, according to his own account, was the overthrow of the existing democracies by revolution fomented as a result of war. Lozovsky's immediate chief in the comintem, Manouilski, declared at the congress of the Russian communist party, I think it was in March of 1939:
This war will be the most just, the most holy, that has ever been fought in the history of mankind: a war which will necessarily stir up a whole series of revolutionary outbreaks within the enemy ranks, and which will break up and demoralize the ranks of imperialism.
Of course he was branding the democracies as imperialists. A still more remarkable statement, to me at any rate, was made by Stalin on March 10, 1939, addressing the bolshevik congress assembled at that time. Here are his words:
The policy of non-intervention means conniving at aggression, giving free rein to war; reveals an eagerness to allow all the belligerents to sink deeper into the mire of war, to encourage them surreptitiously in this, to allow them to weaken and exhaust one another, and then when they have become weak enough, to appear on the scene with fresh strength; to appear of course "in the interests of peace" and to dictate conditions to the enfeebled belligerents. That policy is cheap and it serves our purpose.
I do not think I need draw the attention of hon. members to the way that policy has been and is now being carried out by Russia, faithfully and to the very letter. If I ever heard of a blueprint of their intentions, that is it. Is it not clear to all that Stalin's statement of policy I just read was almost an exact blueprint of what has taken place since that statement was made in 1939? Does it not also explain Russia's most remarkable attitude in the present Korean conflict where, as the minister said yesterday, Russia is trying to prove that the left hook was knocked out by the jaw? Is it not also a blueprint of what the communists have been doing in this and other countries, ostensibly in the name of peace? What about our peace movements here, and these fellows down in Toronto who for all practical purposes have allied themselves with Moscow? I am reminded at this point that in 1939, when Canada was discussing whether our manpower should be sent to Europe to fight Hitler, Moscow's agent in Canada, Tim Buck, declared that not a man should be sent to fight the German fuehrer. It would be, he said, an imperialistic war, and we should not
128	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Low take part in any such war. When Germany attacked Russia a little later on, however, Tim Buck threw a circus somersault, just one of the many he has thrown, and urged that Canada go all-out in sending men and material to fight Hitler. That is the old line, just exactly what Stalin said should be done. Now we have this same communist and his friends in Canada talking about peace. This, of course, fits in with Stalin's remarks, which I read a moment ago, and certainly we can easily imagine the kind of peace they are after.
Well, Russia has taken a number of steps towards dominating Europe and Asia, as was predicted by Stalin. In the light of this situation and in the light of the minister's statement yesterday afternoon that there is grave danger of an uprising in western Germany, this prediction, when it appeared in an English journal on September 16, 1939, seems to me more than significant:
The Russian attitude toward the Hitler regime will he liquidated and Germany, presented with an active enemy on the Polish frontier, will find herself between two fires, a position impossible to defend. Disorder and revolution in Germany will unseat a deflated Hitler. Reconstruction, and a new and convenient note on the propaganda organ, with perhaps a touch of the whip of financial deflation, will convince the Germans of the essential unity of their ideals with mother Russia.
That has been before us ever since 1939. I wonder how much attention we have been paying to such declarations. Is that not exactly what has been happening? Well, with all these things as common knowledge, boldly printed in black and white for all to read and know, it is hard for me to understand why President Roosevelt and Mr. Churchill allowed themselves to be so badly beaten and misled at Yalta and Potsdam. In the light of Russia's oft and openly expressed policies, why did they allow these things to happen, for instance? And I am only quoting a few. First, why did they allow Russia several weeks of sole occupation of Berlin before the allied troops moved in? Second, why did they allow the partition of Berlin in such a way as to leave no corridor of approach, which made possible the Russian blockade of 1948-49? To beat that blockade, as hon. members recall, required a tremendous expenditure of money, material and manpower by the western powers, which was bound to weaken them. Why was the dividing line between eastern and western Berlin drawn in such a way as to give the Russian zone all the power plants for the whole city, so they could torment the citizens of west Berlin by turning off the power whenever they wanted to cause an incident? Third, why did Churchill and Roosevelt allow the partition of Germany and Korea in such a way as to make possible the building up of huge communist armies in each of these countries?


From this terrible mistake, called by the minister yesterday a matter of unfortunate military convenience, has directly stemmed the present Korean aggression and the situation in eastern Germany, which holds a constant threat of war and aggression in Europe. Fourth, why did Roosevelt and Churchill agree to the dismantling of so many of the German industrial plants in 1947 and 1948? I believe on another occasion in this house I mentioned that I saw a number of these plants in the Ruhr valley being dismantled, some of them being sent to such countries as Yugoslavia and Greece, finding their way behind the iron curtain where they could be seized and used by Russia whenever she pleased. Yesterday the minister said:
It is no longer a question of whether Germany is to be rearmed, because the communist part of Germany is already rearmed ... if western Germany is to be defended, it must be given arms with which to assist in its own defence.
I say we must be mighty careful about rearming Germany, because I am satisfied that a rearmed Germany would try it again. Then one recalls that one of President Roosevelt's chief aides, in fact the man who arranged the Yalta conference and who stood at his shoulder during that fateful meeting, was Alger Hiss. One does not forget, either, that when Hiss was convicted, nearly two years ago, of being one of the top communists in the United States he was warmly defended by Acheson, the present secretary of state. I am sure a person might be forgiven for wondering if Mr. Acheson is also, willingly or unwillingly, a protege of the Wall street gang which has been so anxious to promote war and revolution as a means of bringing power and profit to its members.
I am reminded at this point of an article that appeared in the New York Herald Tribune of June 27, 1932, written by none other than Walter Lippmann, in which he said:
It is evident that Roosevelt is not the leader of the forces behind him; he is being used.
A responsible man like Walter Lippmann must have had some reason for making such a statement. I do not know whether it was true, but I believe it could be shown quite easily that America has been the largest contributor to the building up of Russia's huge war-making industrial machine. That has not been with the sanction of the American people as a whole, for whom I have the highest possible regard, but most certainly it has been through the intrigue of a small group who have been in a position to dictate policy. I think it would be most useful and revealing to find out just who has been dictating American policy in this respect. A close study of Russo-American

history, I am sure, would reveal the true enemies of civilization, and I think we should be getting after them. At Easter, 1929, Bertrand Russell is reported to have said that a world war would start during 1939 from which America and Russia would emerge as dictators of the world. He added that the conflict would reduce Germany, Italy, France and England to ruins. I leave hon. members to judge for themselves whether or not Bertrand Russell was in the know.
Much more could be said to indicate how Russia has grown to be a threat to the rest of the world. However, I think I should now say in a few words how we view the present situation. In reality we are facing the most dangerous situation we have ever faced in our history, and somehow we have got to meet it. I quite agree with the minister of external affairs that this grave danger cannot be overcome by military action alone. I agree with the member for Rosetown-Biggar that we have got to use other methods as well, and give all the aid we can to the other parts of the world that require to be brought up to a decent standard of living.
From a military point of view, of course, Canada must be ready to defend herself against acts of aggression that appear possible. Canada must also be ready to fulfil every obligation that devolves upon her as a member of the United Nations so long as she remains a member of that organization. In 1945 we became a signatory to the San Francisco charter. I say that as long as we are members it is up to us to see to it that every one of our obligations is fulfilled. It is to be regretted in the extreme that every nation who signed that charter has not lived up to its obligations. If they had the United States would not have had to stand alone all these weeks in Korea.
The nations who are parties to the San Francisco charter are facing the most serious test that they have ever faced. They must now demonstrate to the whole world that they are capable of effective collective action to put down aggression wherever or whenever it may raise its head. If they do not, then world conflict is bound to be brought many steps closer to us. It does seem unfortunate that the free nations find it so difficult to co-operate with one another in the interests of world peace, and to move swiftly when danger appears. It is difficult to find the root cause of this inability of the free nations to rise quickly in collective action. As a general rule democracy is slow to get into high gear. In addition to that all of our educational systems in the various 69262-9
The Address-Mr. Low free nations have, for many decades, been training the youth in the arts of competition almost to the entire neglect of co-operation.
I need not remind hon. members that nations become nothing but the sum total of the attitudes and ways of the individuals who make up those nations. If the nations of the world now are ever to be able to take collective action against aggression that will preserve their freedoms and the way of life each wants, they must see that individual citizens are trained in the true art of cooperation. I feel sure that the Canadian people will be prepared to give their very best efforts in every way to meet the challenge of these times. Even if the decisions taken at this session do have, as they doubtless will have, serious effects upon the living standards and the lives of all Canadians, I am sure that our people will carry their burdens without murmuring, provided they are made to feel that their grievances are removed in so far as they can be; and provided they feel that the cause for which they struggle and work is a righteous cause. Let us be sure it is righteous.
We are prepared to support the government in building up Canada's defence to the point where we are making the wisest possible use of all of our resources. It is well known that the Social Credit organization has always considered that our efforts to bring security to our own people, and peace to the rest of the world, should be limited only by the extent of our total resources. They are vast resources, as has already been said. We also believe that there must be the utmost of speed in putting Canada into the strongest position necessary to meet whatever will have to be met. It is out belief that the Prime Minister and his colleagues were wise in not sending the small regular Canadian army for service in Korea. That is a job for a special force of another character entirely. Whether or not the new special force that is being recruited proves to be the type of force I shall not be able to say until I get more details.
I am not one, sir, who feels that a world war is inevitable. On the contrary, I feel confident that a world war can be averted, especially if the united free nations of the world take effective action now to put down this aggression in Korea and to see to it that a settlement is made afterward that will satisfy the Koreans. I would suggest, too, that if the united free nations of the world would set up a brigade of honest men-not a brigade in the military sense of the word- and charge them with the responsibility of hunting out and putting the spotlight on the

The Address-Mr. Pearkes real enemies of civilization and disarming them of their forces, then the world could build a real and lasting peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the amendment which was proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) this afternoon, I propose to show that His Excellency's advisers have failed to provide adequately for the defence of Canada. I shall confine my remarks to that portion of the amendment which refers directly to the defence forces of this country. I shall not touch upon the second part of the amendment, although that is closely related to the first part. Others will follow who will deal with the second part.
Yesterday we listened to the speeches of two cabinet ministers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) gave us an historical review of the various events leading up to the present aggression in Korea, and he also gave us some insight into one or two aspects of government foreign policy. I shall long remember his address owing to the quantity and quality of the adjectives which were included in his remarks. I should like to thank the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) for his kindly reference to myself. In his usual clear and concise manner he, in his speech, confirmed all the recent press releases which have been made by his department.
Mr. Speaker, the material of those speeches was not good enough. The members had a right to expect a great deal more. We have travelled from all parts of Canada, at considerable inconvenience to ourselves and at great expense to the public. We had a right to be given more concrete information as to the course this government proposes to follow in these critical times.
After the review of the historic events leading up to the Korean crisis, the Secretary of State for External Affairs informed us that the invasion of the republic of South Korea was an act of aggression. It is true that it was an act of aggression. I wish he had emphasized still more that it was an act of aggression not merely against a satellite of the United States but against a country in which the United Nations have a special interest. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) this afternoon stressed that point, and I think it is one of the outstanding points of interest in connection with

this whole matter because it is the United Nations who guaranteed the independence of Korea.
It was my privilege to stand at the entrance to Esquimau harbour and to see the three Canadian destroyers leave the shores of Canada to sail across the broad waters of the Pacific. I was thrilled. The navy had done a first-rate job in getting those three destroyers ready in the week's time that they had available to them. Changes in command of, I think, every vessel were necessary. It was essential that the ships' companies be completed by withdrawing key personnel from the cruiser Ontario and other vessels and from shore establishments. The vessels had to be supplied with victuals and with ammunition. Yet they left on time. It was a proud moment for all those who saw those vessels leave. We were proud of our Canadian navy, proud of our men who were manning those vessels, and proud, at that time, that Canada was prepared to play her part in what appeared to be the first United Nations effort to stop aggression. Then as those vessels vanished out of sight, or a couple of days later, when we saw the cruiser Ontario return to Esquimau harbour, the people of British Columbia began to realize that they had then no defence of the west coast of this country. Their only active destroyers had gone. The Ontario, a training ship, her crew depleted, her personnel made up of reservists, was returning. Had there been enemy submarines in those waters or if enemy submarines appeared in those waters today, the Ontario must withdraw behind the anti-submarine nets and stay in Esquimau harbour. It would be suicide to send her, a training ship, out unescorted by destroyers, without proper protection, against enemy submarines. I repeat that the west coast is defenceless as far as the navy is concerned.
Then we thought of the air. We have in Vancouver one regular air squadron whose duty is to carry out search and rescue work in connection with accidents at sea. We have an auxiliary fighting squadron made up of personnel who, in the ordinary course of events, go about their ordinary civilian avocations and give such time as they can to training and manning of the aircraft. They have two or three Vampire planes, two jet planes with which to defend the hundreds of miles of dangerous, indented British Columbian coast. That is the situation which exists today and which the people of British Columbia now realize exists.
When this matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of National Defence some sort of press release was issued to the

effect that if there was any trouble the United States navy would be there ready to help us. Do not forget that the major units of the United States navy, which are normally stationed in American Pacific waters, are today in the Far East off Korea, watching the straits between the mainland of China and Formosa and guarding the sea lanes in the Far East. They are not at hand in great numbers ready and available to intercept anything which might be threatening the coast of British Columbia. The other day we listened to an outline of the new auxiliary air squadrons which the minister intends to establish. I listened intently to hear whether the appeals of the ex-flying men of British Columbia had been answered, and whether included amongst the new auxiliary air force squadrons would be the squadron which Victoria has been appealing to the minister year after year to have supplied. But there was no mention of it. I repeat that the coast line of British Columbia is defenceless and steps must be taken without delay to make good the deficiencies which already exist. It is too great a risk to ask the people of British Columbia to run. I know that you will say the Pacific coast is the back door of Canada. The main entrance today is on the Atlantic, but the enemy which we face lurks in the alleyways instead of parading down the highways of this world.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) went on with his historical review I noticed that little, nay no, mention was made of that urgent appeal which was sent out by General MacArthur, and repeated a few days later from the United Nations, asking for ground troops to be sent without delay in order to assist the United States forces in their life and death struggle in Korea. Why did the minister skate around that all-important point? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it took the government almost a month to make up its mind whether it would respond to that urgent appeal from our greatest neighbour, the one to whom we have been turning and so frequently mentioning in the last few years, saying that we counted upon her to come to our help if we should be in trouble. The government took almost a month before it decided that it would provide troops to go to her assistance, to respond to what I think I may say was a pathetic appeal for help.
Then we were told that the army was not prepared; that we had no troops that we could send to answer that appeal. The Minister of National Defence said that the supplying of forces to do police work for the United Nations against an aggressor was not part of our defence program. There was no promise that 69262-9J
The Address-Mr. Pearkes it would be done, and there was no suggestion that we should prepare to do it. I take issue with and challenge the correctness of that statement. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave the hint this afternoon that such matters had been discussed when he said that they asked for specific instructions as far back as 1946 as to what role Canada should play, but the specific instructions then were not available.
It is less than a year since the Minister of National Defence tabled his white paper in which the objectives of the defence of Canada were outlined. Talking about what had happened in the past he mentions Canada's defence purposes on page 11, and he-names them one, two and three. The third objective reads:
To work out with other free nations plans for joint defence based on self-help and mutual aid as part of a combined effort to preserve peace and ter restrain aggression.
I cannot reconcile those two statements', that this was not part of our plans when a year ago the minister published that. He cannot convince me that with such a clear directive given to the chiefs of staff, with the knowledge that they had of the events which have taken place in Greece, in Malaya and the Dutch East Indies, they would be so remiss in their duties that they would not have made plans for just such an eventuality as is happening now in Korea. I know these men. I have known them for years. I have more confidence in their integrity, in their loyalty and in their devotion to this country than to think that they would have overlooked such an elementary problem.
The government decided that it would raise a special force. It would go slow and adopt the casual procedure of creating an entirely new and improvised force, drawn not from men who had been accustomed to working with their officers, but men drawn from the streets, from this and that battalion, if they had been overseas veterans, from this and that unit of the reserve army, or schoolboys coming out of the universities through the C.O.T.C.
The appeal was made to the young men of Canada. That appeal has been magnificently responded to. But what have we got? A conglomeration of men bearing the proud names of great units, unknown to their own special unit commanders, their officers, their N.C.O's. Any man who has had any experience in the service will tell you that it takes a long time to weld such groups of men together in order that they become a fighting team, because it is teamwork that counts, not merely the individual skill of an individual soldier tp handle his weapon.

The Address-Mr. Pearkes
This government has created a new Kitchener's army-

-with all the mistakes that were made in 1914 when these hastily raised units were created. We now have a dual service army. It is no good for the minister to say that it is not so; the service conditions are different.
Reference was made to the airborne brigade. The airborne brigade is composed of magnificent units with long traditions in the service of Canada. The personnel are of the finest physique, of the strongest character. There could not be found a better type of young Canadian from the Atlantic to the Pacific; but it is no good, and it is not right that the minister should burden them with a reputation for efficiency that they have never had a chance of reaching.
Reference was made to the degree of training the airborne brigade has received. There is no headquarters. No headquarters have been trained to command the various units. There is no staff appointed. There is no signals section working with the units. Those units have never been brought together as units to take part in any formation exercise. You are saddling those men with an unfair burden if you are telling the people of Canada that they are a fully-trained operational formation. They are the grandest men there are in Canada, but their position has not been fairly represented to the people of Canada. Trained in unit exercises?-yes. Trained in the individual use of their weapons?-yes but not trained'-no training commenced-as an airborne brigade or to fight together as component units of a brigade. The best that could be done, if they were called upon to go into action, would be to pour those units or sub-units into the battle piecemeal. Today they could not fight coherently because they have never been trained to act as a formation.
Again, are there suitable aircraft either to transport or to escort them? I think it is only right that the impression which was created or the impression which may have been drawn from the remarks made yesterday by the minister should be corrected.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) referred to the fact that there might be other acts of aggression. I think that is very likely. He referred to the possibility of acts of aggression, other Koreas, may I say, occurring in various parts of the world -in Persia, in Iran, in Malaya. He did not mention that such acts of aggression might occur in Canada. That day, that seemingly carefree day when, complacently, we could say that the only possible attack on Canada would be that of a diversionary raid, has

gone, and has gone for all time. Canada today is vulnerable to operations of much greater magnitude than any diversionary raid which might be checked by a few northern rangers or a couple of hundred men of the active army.
It is my considered opinion that this country is vulnerable, and that it is eminently practicable for a ruthless enemy to start an act of aggression against portions of this continent of a very much graver nature than could possibly be described as a diversionary raid.
You say: "How can that be done? It is not practicable." I referred a moment ago to the fact that we have no navy on the Pacific coast. The waters of the Pacific are wide. There is much close weather in the Pacific. It is not impracticable for a detachment of a foreign navy to cross the Pacific, unknown to such watching troops as there are available, and to reach the shores of British Columbia before effective opposition could be brought to bear-to land troops at, say, Prince Rupert. You laugh? May I remind hon. members that the American navy was closely watching the island of Kiska in the Aleutians, but the Japanese garrison slipped away under the very nose of that American fleet-and that was not a hundred men or so, but a couple of thousand men. And they did not leave by submarine or rowboat; they were transported by armed transports.
Those are things we must bear in mind. Distances have been eliminated. Airborne formations in great numbers are possible, provided the enemy is ruthless and is not particular about the losses he may suffer. And is the enemy the Americans are facing today callous or not callous about the number of casualties he suffers?
In his speech the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said there has been a good summer training for the reserve force. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there has been a good summer "for" training; that is what he should have said. Why is it that there has not been a good summer training? The weather was fine; the camps were there; the equipment was there; the instructors were there. But there was a lack of manpower in the reserve units.
Here and there, scattered across this *country, are certain reserve units which were able to go into camp at reasonably high strength. There were many other units that failed to take 25 per cent of their establishment into camp. There were other units that failed to take in 10 per cent, or even 5 per cent. I can name some of them. I saw some of those units with my own eyes.

A unit which has not trained 10 per cent of its establishment can hardly be considered in any standard of preparedness. I do suggest the money spent on units which cannot come up to a standard of efficiency is not well spent. They cannot take the field in any reasonable time after a crisis has occurred. It would be better to send the few men of those units through the excellent basic and corps training camps that were established in this country during the last war. I do not believe money spent on that type of unit is justified, or gives adequate returns to the public for the money they are spending in that direction.
Then may we ask why? Why is it that we see this weakness in so many units? I have had reports from all over the country-I am not speaking of one isolated district. Mr. Speaker, it is because this government has failed to impress upon the country the seriousness of the present situation. The speeches which have been made in this house time and time again have encouraged a spirit of complacency which has had an effect upon recruiting for the reserve units of our services. I placed a very different interpretation upon the remarks made this afternoon by my leader than the interpretation attributed to those remarks by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he spoke afterward. My leader was sounding a grave warning, he was uttering a fervent prayer and expressing a belief that if a change was to take place, if there was real co-operation, if the people of the free countries became alive to the situation, there might be a chance of a third world war not taking place.
But there was a big "if". There have been five years of ceaseless effort to disrupt the economies of the democracies; there have been five years of manufactured revolutions by which puppet states have been set up all over this world; there have been five years of violence and murder in the colonial dependencies of many of the democracies, all of which should have taught us that we are face to face with a calculated and determined conspiracy restricted by no moral obligations whatsoever and with a potential military strength of one-third of the human race, a conspiracy which is determined upon the destruction of democracy and of both the Christian and Jewish faiths in order that a communist slave state may be established over the whole of this planet.
It is only a matter of time before that challenge has to be accepted if the free world is to survive. Therefore it seems to me that the problem facing the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and this government can be placed under three headings. First,
The Address-Mr. Pearkes there is the Korea of today. I am of the opinion that we have missed an opportunity to give world leadership in that respect. I fear that the brigade now in training will be ready, either too late or just in time to take part in the victory parade.
The second point is that there will be other acts of aggression in other parts of the world, not excluding Canada. In order to meet those acts of aggression we must have troops, including ground troops, in being. Then there is the third phase. It may be, and we hope, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has said, we may be able to educate the lesser countries, the countries which have not the same opportunities we have, that we may be able to raise their standards of living. But, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs says, that will take generations, and I believe that will be the case.
It is quite possible that Russia thinks she is working toward the same ends, but time is against Russia. As my leader said, we are working on borrowed time. I am inclined to think that Russia will attempt to bring on this final phase at the earliest possible opportunity as soon as she is ready. Russia will not delay because the years will work in favour of the democracies. If this final phase should come we cannot match manpower with manpower, we cannot arm with bayonets and clubs the soldiers of the democracies to meet the bayonets and clubs in the hands of the great human masses now under the control of Russia.
But we have a weapon in which we are superior to the Russians, namely, the brains and ability of our people to put into effect the industrial resources of this country. I believe that it will be with brains and machines that we shall ultimately gain the victory if we are forced into this final phase. As was shown this afternoon, there are great numbers of Russian divisions already poised in western Europe. It may well be that those Russian divisions will overrun western Europe, in which event we may find that this northern part of the American continent will be the armed airport and arsenal of the world from which eventually great air fleets would carry on a final offensive in order to regain the world for democracy and Christianity.
We must be prepared to meet those three eventualities. It will require wise judgment and a nice sense of balance to see that we do not place too much emphasis on one or the other phase. I feel that to date the government has failed to inform this nation either of the seriousness of the situation as

The Address-Mr. Gillis it exists in the world today or of the weaknesses of our own defence forces. I am sincere when I say that I sympathize with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) because of the difficulties with which he is faced. He has an extremely heavy task to perform. While 1 have found it necessary to speak as I have today I believe we should give every possible assistance in the preparation of our services as they are organized under the responsibility of the present government.
But I appeal to the minister never again to present to this house such a speech as he made yesterday. All is not well. Neither the purchase of obsolescent aircraft from the United States or elsewhere nor the exaggerated claims as to the efficiency of our equipment or our standards of training and the excellence of our own men will correct the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to both the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton); and what I have to say in regard to the program and policy they placed before this house I trust will not be taken as criticism. As I see it these ministers are in pretty much the same position as a boxer in the ring. They have to do the fighting; they have the responsibility. When a boxer is in the ring a fellow at the ringside can give him a lot of good advice, to use his left, to use his right and so on; but the guy in the ring has a face full of gloves and is not in a very good position to take that advice. However, I would like to say a few things in regard to both speeches.
This is not an ordinary session of parliament. We are meeting at the call of the cabinet to deal with two emergencies. One of them we have succeeded in settling. The settlement was not exactly to my liking; nevertheless the trains are running again. In my opinion, however, the basic cause that put them off the tracks still remains, and until its roots are pulled out we are not going to remove that cause. The second matter considered an emergency-and it is an emergency-is the international situation as it affects this country. That matter is far from settled.
The first thing I want to point out is the responsibility of members themselves. I am rather disappointed at the rush to get the business concluded and the members back home. There may be various reasons for this, but I believe a basic reason is that we are

still trying to function with the kind of parliament which was designed to look after the conditions of 1867; and we do not have that kind of world any longer. This matter of running a fifteen billion dollars a year business for the Canadian people is a fulltime job, not one requiring attention only during the months we are here. I do not think the average member of parliament can continue to carry on as he did even ten or fifteen years ago, and just come in and take some responsibility while the house is in session. We are not running Canada alone; we are dealing with one world. If members of this house are to properly represent their people, keep them advised and carry them along in the changing conditions they have to continually study what is going on in the world as it relates to this country. I think hon. members will have to make up their minds either to run the business for the people of Canada as it must be run today, or to go back home and run some other kind of business for themselves. For the next few years, at least as I see things developing in the world, the constant attention of members of this house will be required, with a great deal of reading and studying in order to keep our people informed.
If that is not done we will find that our cabinets will last only about four or five years. I do not think any men who have to work as I have seen the cabinet work for the last number of years will last much longer than that. Physically it cannot be done. They are not working a thirty or forty hour week.
