The same thing applies to any member of this house who takes his responsibility seriously. He is in this building at least by nine o'clock in the morning and is here until eleven-thirty every night; and that is not a thirty-hour week. I am sure the older members of this house who have been here for some considerable time have seen a number of members of the cabinet wear out.
But we are not only overloading the cabinet in the matter of the hours they must put in and the pressure they must withstand; we are handing over to the civil service the rest of the job of running the country. We are building up a bureaucracy behind the scenes who, because we are not prepared to stay here and accept our responsibilities, must run the country in accordance with decisions we may have made months ago which perhaps have no bearing on the immediate problems with which they are confronted. Unless we are prepared to seriously consider the job of being a member of this house, in the sort of

world we are living in today, with the responsibilities we have to accept, as a full-time job, we had better not undertake it at all. If any hon. member comes in here with the idea that he wants to get out again as quickly as possible, in order to operate a business back home or something like that, then he is not doing either for his own business back home or for this country the sort of thing he should be doing. We should make up our minds to that. I may not be the brightest person in the world, but I know it takes me some considerable time to get straight in my own mind the things I know I should be thinking about. I cannot do it overnight, and I think most hon. members are in the same position.
I believe that is the first thing we must do in the light of the developing international situation. We in this house must act as a liaison between ourselves, the government and the people of Canada, because in the final analysis it is the people of Canada who will have to pay the taxes, who will have to do the fighting if fighting must be done, and who will have to produce the wherewithal to permit that fighting to be done. They should be kept informed, not by way of propaganda but by giving them the unvarnished facts, because in this kind of world you cannot fool people for very long.
Then if we are serious about making our maximum contribution in future, and if we are to have a realistic international policy, I believe we must get our own house in order, for I believe that what you do internationally is determined by what you are doing internally. If you have a chaotic, upset condition within your own country you are not going to be able to make your maximum contribution to the work of the United Nations. In that connection I would remind hon. members that last week we had a serious disruption of our entire economy. That disruption was not brought about for fun. The men engaged in it were serious people. It happened because a certain group in our society were still receiving substandard wages, and every time they picked up a newspaper or listened to the radio they were told that sugar was in short supply; that prices were going up; that butter was going up, tea was going up, and so on. In the last six months a terrific increase has taken place in the cost of the things that go on the table of the average man; and eighty per cent of the income of the average salary or wage earner in this country is spent on the essentials that go on his table. So the increase in the cost of foodstuffs alone has put a terrific strain upon those who are producing the wealth of this country; and that group in
The Address-Mr. Gillis that sector of our society, regardless of international affairs or wars or anything else, went on strike and the economy of the country was disrupted. Secondly, that is not going to stop there unless we do something about the root cause, and the root cause is inflationary prices. In this country it has taken us since 1945 to persuade some of the unions in the basic industries that long-term contracts were necessary. In my opinion a year's contract is no good. The ink on it is scarcely dry before you get into another fight. Some of the unions did do that. The mine workers, for example, signed a two-year agreement, and the auto workers signed a five-year agreement. As soon as we get that problem in the right focus, away go prices.
The argument one now hears everywhere is that we signed an agreement on the expectation that the government would at least see that prices were kept within reasonable limits. As soon as we tie ourselves to a five-year agreement, away go prices and we lose everything we gained within the last two or three years. If we are a responsible union we are tied to that contract, and we cannot violate it. There is unrest in the steel industry because the conciliation board has not been successful. Steel is basic to our economy. One of our first jobs is to see that the economy of this country is arranged in such a way that it is not going to be disrupted and interfere with our commitments in the international field. Those commitments will not wait. We are not the aggressor. If we are going to make our maximum contribution in the international field, then we have to see that our own economy is regulated and geared to maximum production. We have to see that there is no possibility of disruption as we go along. That is not very difficult because the price control machinery is there. It is just a matter of taking it out of mothballs. The excess profits tax legislation can be looked at.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) says that he wants more taxes. With prices skyrocketing people are going to wonder if income taxes are increased but nothing is done about excess profits taxes. I believe those things are absolutely necessary at this time. Our first step towards doing a good job outside is to get our own economy in order, as an example to those outside that we are able to run our own show.

He is not doing so badly. Facts and figures bear that out. As I was saying, I think our first job is to see that our own house is put in order.
In connection with this matter of national defence, I may say that I listened to the minister's speech. I believe he was badly advised at the last session of the house when he refused to implement the proposal for a national defence committee. In the light of what has happened in the last couple of months, I believe that if the minister had been in the position to call in that committee to share the responsibility for the development of defence equipment, he would have relieved himself of a great burden. Making the members on this side take some responsibility is not a bad way of neutralizing opposition. The minister did not do that. I believe it still should be done. Then, too, I believe the minister used bad psychology during his radio broadcast concerning the new defence force, the police force. As I recall it, he had this to say. He said the special force we will be raising will not be drawn from the regular forces. The army we have in Canada now, and the air force, is going to remain in Canada for the defence of Canada. This new force is going to receive a certain amount of training, and will be available to this international police force.
I know the minister meant well, but here is the reaction his words created throughout the country. I know it was my reaction. I said, "Yes, that is not a bad arrangement." We have filled up the chairs with brigadiers and generals; we have set up a good professional army in Canada with men who came out of universities. We have given them training for the last five or six years, and now that there is some fighting to be done they are going to stay home and defend Canada. We are going to pick the little fellow out of the ranks of the unemployed, put him in uniform and send him out. That may not have been the minister's intention, but I am telling the minister that was my reaction, and that was the reaction of the average man in the street. I heard such comments everywhere I went. Whether or not we like it, that is poor psychology.
I believe we have fallen down on the job in this matter of defence. When the United Nations charter came before this house we were definitely told that under this arrangement the military staff of the different countries would meet, and an international police force would be selected. I know that was not done because, as I understand it,


every obstacle was put in the way by the U.S.S.R. We know why Russia did that. On the other hand Russia organized her police force in country after country. She was using the satellite countries to build up armies. At the same time the commonwealth group, instead of doing what we said we were going to do under the UN, did nothing. Surely we did not expect that our obligation was going to end because Russia did not want us to do anything about it. This force should have been organized five or six years ago. When the Korean affair started this country, Britain, the United States and other commonwealth countries should have had a force ready to send there. I know it was a shock to me, as it was to a lot of other people, to find the security council of the United Nations acting as quickly as it did. But when a definite decision was made that an act of aggression had been committed in Korea, there was no force available to send there. The other fellow had his army ready, his tanks and his equipment, but the UN had nothing except the token force sent by the United States.
I believe both the United States and ourselves have fallen down badly on this matter of defence. We should have had some force ready. No purpose is served in holding a post mortem over the thing. From now on we have to recognize the fact, as I said a moment ago, that we are not living in the Canada in which we were living ten years ago. If you read that book written by the late Wendell Willkie after his tour of the world, you will find that he definitely stated we are living in one world. What happens in one part affects the other part. It is too bad that man did not live, because he would have been a valuable person in the world today. In that book he clearly visualized the development of the world.
We have been lulled into complacency by the fact that we have been living close-to the United States all this time, and there are no fortifications on the border. There is no fear of aggression from that direction, but the world has shrunk. Despite the fact that we are not afraid of the United States, Korea, China, Greece, Germany and every other part of the world today offers opportunity for aggression at any time they feel like moving; and we must recognize the fact that we have got to keep our outposts up and be ready to go to the assistance of those outposts at any time that it is necessary.
In Korea itself I think the lesson taught there is one that should be learned. We have had five years in that part of the world. When the war finished in 1945 the United Nations divided that country in two, or at least they followed out the terms of the agreement in setting up the spheres of influence, Russia

on one side and the United States on the other. We had five years under a UN commission in Korea. Russia did what she should do according to her program if she intends to dominate the world. She put in technical personnel. She built up an army. She trained that army and she put guns and ammunition in their hands to move forward when they were ready.
On the other hand, what did the United States do or what did we ourselves do? The United States army stayed in there for a while. They developed some kind of mechanics. They got some kind of government functioning, and I am not being too critical about that because a country that was under the domination of Japan since 1904 could have little idea of the mechanics of democracy or the functioning of government. But they picked up what they could, and unfortunately they picked up people who were trained in the wrong kind of way by the Japanese when they occupied that part of the country.
Ever since the formation of the South Korean government there has been a great deal of criticism-and that criticism has come from people like ourselves, not rank leftists or anything of that kind-about the way in which things were done in South Korea. For example, instead of getting in people who would develop democracy from the bottom, they were trying to impose it from the top. I myself saw a report by a man who was well informed and who went into that part of the country as a trade union expert, with the intention of developing the trade union movement; and that is the basis of democracy in any country. What happened? He got nowhere there. Everybody in Korea who did not agree with Syngman Rhee was considered to be a communist.
The part of this report which I read in some of the American papers was to the effect that in the last year, or in one year, over
150,000	people were jailed in that country because they expressed opinions different from the opinions of those who were in power. We did not develop democracy there. We pulled out and we left it wide open, with a discontented people. As a result, we are paying for that mistake. As for myself, I think that what we must do in the future is this. When you take over a country such as Korea, instead of occupying it and trying to impose a government from the top, the mechanics of democracy must be developed from the bottom. As this chap, Stanley Earl, pointed out in his report, you cannot develop democracy by means of cocktail parties and just meeting with the bankers' association. That is 69262-10
The Address-Mr. Gillis the kind of thing he ran up against. He finally left altogether and came back to the United States a few months ago.
That is the kind of thing that was going on there. That is why the token forces the Americans have had there have had things so tough. I myself think they have been sabotaged from top to bottom. A good deal of that could have been avoided if, back in 1945, 1946, and 1947, people who really intended to develop democracy in that country had gone in there and shown the Korean people, the peasants and the workers of Korea who had been exploited, kicked around and mistreated by the Japanese since 1904 that we really came in as their liberators and intended to develop within that country a united nation under the United Nations. But that was not done. I think we must benefit by that mistake.
Do not forget that the appeal that Russia is making to the average man today is exactly the same as the one that Hitler made. Hitler's only appeal to oppressed people was: Give up your freedom and in return we will give you security. That was the appeal that he made. When people are starved, jailed and mistreated, they will try anything. That is why China capitulated as fast as she did. There must be the will to fight. People must have something to fight for. It is just not good enough to be against something, for one to say that he is against communism or against fascism. I think we have got to be for something; and in my opinion that something is this. We have got to go in there, establish democracy, raise living standards, make these people part of a world organization and give them something to fight for. Otherwise the road ahead is going to be fairly tough.
We might as well realize-and I am quite frank in my thinking about it-that for the rest of our lives we are going to have high taxes and standing armies, not for the purpose of aggression but for the purpose of defending ourselves, because the people we are dealing with today, namely the Soviet union, have not any intention of stopping. All of this nonsense that their representative talks at the United Nations and all of the other propaganda you get all over the country, and which is fooling a great many people, does not fool anyone who knows the program and policy of that party. They say definitely, and have said so for a long time, that the system of capitalism and communism cannot exist in the one world. One has to go.
Here are some figures I picked up in the press, as given by defence minister Emanuel

The Address-Mr. Gillis Shinwell to the House of Commons in Britain. He reported that Russia had 2,800,000 men under arms; that she maintains an army of 175 active divisions, of which one-third are mechanized; that she has 19,000 military planes, including jet aircraft of the latest design, both bombers and fighters; that she has 25,000 tanks; that she could double her 2,800,000-man standing army by calling up reserves; that she has considerable naval forces which include strong fleets of submarines, many of them of modern design; and that she is spending not less than 13 per cent of her national income on her armed forces. They are not doing that for fun.
In addition to that potential within the borders of Russia itself, you have the satellite countries to contend with; and in the period that Russia is in today, she is not going to use any of her own forces. This is the period they designed as the period of national revolutions, and they are running according to schedule. They are promoting the thing from the inside. They are softening up their victims. They are holding their own forces in reserve but they are using the satellites. They will fight in Korea to the last Chinaman, as far as Russia is concerned. They will do the same in any other country; and when they get it properly messed up and softened up, that huge force within the borders of Russia itself is there to be used. That is what we are up against and we might as well realize that. I think the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) might as well realize that also; and I think the members of this House of Commons had better realize it and see that their people back home understand it, because we must have their understanding co-operation. We have either got to beat that machine or that machine is going to beat us. That is the basis on which we have got to do our thinking today. I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and others this afternoon and also the Secretary of State for External Affairs were realistic when they said that military strength is not enough. We must have an economic program to support it, because the greatest weapon we have in Asia, and in many sections of Europe, is the sending of foodstuffs to them. If we consider the fact that from 40 per cent to 45 per cent of the present world's production is being produced on this continent and we have only 7 per cent of the world's population to use it, we will see that the huge surpluses that can be produced on this continent must be sent out. These figures, brief as they are, indicate also the complete lack of the necessities of life in other parts of the world. Whoever gets in there first and feeds and clothes these people

will have their support. Talking about longterm investments in other countries, I do not care whether it is a gift because if we give it away it is an insurance that at least you are going to live the normal span of life, you are going to be alive on this continent anyway for the next twenty-five or thirty years. If we do not give it away, if we do not assist these backward countries, someone else is going to go in and do it at the point of a gun, and at the point of a gun these people are going to come to this part of the world where there is something to eat.
We had better learn that lesson and take the advice of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and others who have stated realistically that we should get down to business, get an economic and social program and extend it to other parts of the world that are badly in need of it, so that we may have their friendship and their support in the world to come to face the machine that has been developed in Russia for the purpose of destroying everything that exists on this continent.
The thing that is necessary now, Mr. Speaker, if we mean business, is to shake off whatever complacency we have, because this is not the time for it. Every hon. member has to consider himself a liaison officer between this House of Commons and what the government is doing, and must do, and the people back home who have to produce the wherewithal. The government immediately must take some steps to control prices, because unless they control prices they will set off a chain reaction such as we had here the other day in steel, coal and other essential commodities. That can be done and done very easily. Then there should be the reimposition of the excess profits tax in order to hold down as low as we possibly can whatever increases may be necessary in the personal income tax. If these things are done and done immediately, and the members of the House of Commons go back and back up that stand and make being a member of parliament a full-time job, they will be assisting greatly in this crisis. You must get out among the people and keep them informed and posted. Do not forget the little firebugs in this country are out all the time. They are not thinking of running a business and making money for themselves. They are thinking about destroying this country, taking this country over and replacing this institution by an institution with one man in it, Tim Buck, who will tell you what to do, and when to get up and what you are going to eat, and so forth. For the next couple of years we have to keep our feet on the ground, get out and do a job among our people to offset the

kind of worm that is undermining the institutions of this country today.

Mr. Speaker, five years have intervened since the conclusion of the last war. We have lived in a world in which hope and fear have been intermingled, hope that we would be spared all the horrors of another war and fear that the exigency of war might again come to us in our lifetime. Sometimes it has been a hope; sometimes it has been a fear. In the recent past there has existed in the democracies the fear that we would again be faced with the dreadful prospect of another war.
If we go back five years we could have at that time, like any democratic nation, adopted one of two attitudes. We could have devoted all our resources and revenues to preparing for another war, or we could have done nothing.
I think that the people of all democracies abhor war. They never like to prepare for war unless they have to do so. The question whether or not we have made a proper approach to the problem has become increasingly important. In my lifetime we have gone through two wars. We were not in fact ready for the other wars at the time at which they actually started. The possibility was contemplated but when they actually became apparent we were not ready. On the other hand I think we came out of those wars as creditably and contributed as much as any nation in the world. Today we should look at the situation as it exists, so far as we can be informed, sanely, coolly and realistically, and try to keep ourselves from being worked into hysteria, which may be characterized toy a lot of sound but which does not solve anything. If we do so we shall see that we have taken a reasonable and longterm approach to this problem. I will make further reference to that later.
I was disturbed to hear the hon, member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) make what I thought was an unfair, not an attack on, but a series of observations about the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs, like his predecessor, the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) during the past four or five years, in fact ever since the last war ended, has kept this country as fully informed as, and probably more fully informed than, most other countries in the world. These gentlemen have been most meticulous to see that every bit of information that could be given to the public was given.
I do not think any secretary of state for external affairs, any more than any other
69262-10i
The Address-Mr. Campney individual, can peer into the future and tell us what is going to happen. All that he can do is to deal with the facts as they develop. There is nothing static about external affairs. They go on from day to day and vary from day to day. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has in my opinion done a marvellous job in keeping this house and the country informed. He has gone further than that. His participation in the activities of the United Nations has made a mark and a contribution to the solution of the world's problems, so far as we have had any solution, and to the progress of our preparedness equal to that of any other foreign minister of the world. His name has become famous throughout the United Nations.
As I recall the debates in the past two or three sessions since I have been a member, the cry of the opposition has been that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has not given information, but has kept all the facts under cover. They complain that they have not been able to find out all the details. Well, there are two sides to that. I took the trouble to look up the British Hansard which dealt with war estimates, army estimates, naval estimates, and air estimates. I looked at the information given. Generally speaking, we certainly have had much more information than that given to the parliament of Great Britain. In the speech which the minister of defence made yesterday we had as fine, as complete and as detailed a presentation of the present proposals with respect to the special force and the proposals with respect to our regular forces, the development with respect to our reserve army and the other services, the navy and the air force, as any person could reasonably expect. I think the presentation of the relevant facts was just as perfect as any minister could be expected to make it in existing circumstances.
One criticism, as I understood it, made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) was that we had been dilatory and ineffective in taking the necessary steps in connection with the special force for service in Korea or in such other part of the world as it might be necessary to use it. The hon. member, I believe, paid a very fine compliment to the men, as men; but he said that the special force was a "conglomeration of men" and, I took it, developed from that suggestion the deduction that it was something of which we might not be too proud.

I do not pretend to have expert knowledge in the matter, but from my observations my associations and contacts I cannot find myself in agreement with what I understood to be the viewpoint of the hon. member for Nanaimo, who I thought disparagingly-and I believe I am using the proper word-referred to the activities of the reserve army.

My information is that in the last year the reserve army has been stepped up tremendously as regards voluntary enlistments, type of training, attendance at camps and other relevant details. It was not very many sessions ago that the hon. member for Nanaimo wanted to scrap the army and direct all our efforts toward the development of an air force. Today, however, it seems he is terribly concerned about the army. My view

would be that we must maintain a balance among all three services; and I think that is what the government is doing.
I had the honour last session to act as chairman of a committee which studied the bill directed to unification of the three services. At that time I was greatly impressed by the scope of the act, the approach to the problem by the government, and particularly by the vision shown by the Minister of National Defence. I was also favourably impressed by the advice of the highly competent persons who were seeking to assist the government as permanent officials in bringing about the desired unification. This, again, was done in anticipation of what might happen, and what we might be called upon to do.
The fact which presents itself most forcibly to my mind is that we do not like war; we are a democratic people; but as we become more and more convinced that a world war might occur we are prepared, within the limits of the resources of our country, to step up our preparation for such a war.
I do not agree at all with the comment of the member for Nanaimo that we have been dilatory in dealing with this matter. I think all hon. members will agree that the only nation that could save the immediate situation as it developed in Korea was the United States. That country had forces nearby, and at one time had been in actual occupation of that country. It is a truism that in a time of difficulty a nation does not commit its troops piecemeal without adequate preparation. The situation has been stabilized, and we are now making a contribution by way of a naval detachment and through our air force to its immediate needs. Within a reasonable period of time we will have a large number of troops available. I am sure that if our force does go to Korea, or wherever it may go, it will give a good account of itself, just as all Canadian units throughout our history have done.
The hon. member for Nanaimo became considerably perturbed over what he described as a very serious situation on the Pacific coast. We are all concerned about the Pacific coast, just as we are all concerned about the whole situation as it applies to the defence of Canada. My understanding is that the situation on the Pacific coast is integrated with the defence scheme of the United States, and that that scheme includes British Columbia, the Yukon and Alaska.
I happen to know something of what has been done out there, and what is now being done. In the light of that knowledge I cannot agree with him when he suggests that the

Pacific coast has been deserted, and makes the further suggestion that the coast is not defensible or that it is not in as good a position as any other part of Canada from the standpoint of defence. It is in fact in a better position than most of Canada.
Let us be practical about this matter. The hon. member for Nanaimo almost brought us, alone, to the verge of war with Russia. We alone cannot hope to win a war against Russia. We can make our contribution only in conjunction with the United States and as a participant in the conduct of any war to which the United Nations may be committed abroad. We must be realistic about this. Indeed, I think with deference that the hon. member for Nanaimo should have addressed most of his speech to the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). While the hon. member for Nanaimo scolds the Minister of National Defence for not having done enough, the hon. member for Kamloops does not think anyone at all should enlist in the special force for Korea or elsewhere. Surely they should get together, because there is here a further obvious indication that the policy of the Progressive Conservative party is gaping at the seams.
In the light of ever-changing world conditions, and indeed the grave changes which take place even from day to day, I believe that this government has taken a sane, intelligent and forward-looking position, and that its action has placed this country in a position where all our available power can speedily be stepped up to meet any situation, and this with a minimum loss of time and a minimum of difficulty.
I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South when he says that in the event of general hostilities a great part of the contribution this country would be able to make to the common cause would be on the industrial front. In that regard I would point out that we still have our former minister of munitions and supply in the saddle, and I do not think that under such circumstances either the hon. member for Cape Breton South or I need worry further on that score.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has said, there must be control of prices. Yesterday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) made it quite clear that there must be preparation on the economic front. I believe that he should realize that the first thing necessary to bring about a sound condition on the economic front is price control or at least stability and equitability of prices to be accomplished either by price control or some other device.
The Address-Mr. Blackmore
Up to the present time the people of my constituency stand absolutely astounded that the government has taken no steps, either directly or in co-operation with the provinces, to do anything at all to meet the rapidly rising price structure. The government acts exactly as though they lived on Mars and the news had not yet got to them that there might be rising prices in Canada.
There is a limit beyond which this kind of abominable thing had better not go! While prices are rising and while occasionally a group of men may strike and get increased wages, the great rank and file of the people have more or less fixed incomes which are altogether inadequate to meet prices as they now exist.
The government seems to be afraid all the time. That is one of the astonishing things. They have been in power for two or three years but they always seem to be afraid to take hold of anything and, to use an agricultural phrase, "sock the levers in" and produce results. They seem to be afraid of spending a little money or making commitments that are going to cost money. They seem to be afraid to run risks. They always-want to put the risk on the other fellow.
It would appear that the agriculturists are being asked to assume all the risks. As an example: the agriculturists in my constituency are taking all the risk. The government will' not help them at all. The government even makes things worse as for instance in allowing freight rates to be increased and thus increasing the price of everything used in production, but they will not do a single solitary thing to help them. We have striking examples of that right now. If this sort of thing is going on all over the country there certainly needs to be a change, and a very rapid and effective change. Otherwise the Minister of National Defence has no chance of having an economic situation suitable to entering another war.
It seems to^ me that the government does not quite realize, although I believe they are trying to realize, the lightning-like rapidity of the onslaught that is likely to occur. For example, supposing an airborne division of Russians lands in the central part of the prairie provinces. It is not going to make known to us by radio or by newspaper report that it is coming. We will get word suddenly that some thousands of men have arrived completely equipped and have dug themselves in. We would then have to get them out.
Several times the minister has endeavoured1 to assure us that there are forces ready to intercept any such attacking force. But when.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore you think of the enormous numbers we may have to meet and about which we heard this afternoon as constituting the forces of Russia I doubt very much that there are forces in Canada capable of intercepting such powers. Of course the ordinary member like myself who has no access to the inside facts finds it quite impossible to present any clear, definite and satisfactory evidence, but judging by the amount of stir visible throughout the country I would say that we are about the quietest country preparing for war that man could imagine. We seem to be in a deep sleep.
Instead of everything being all astir, instead of everybody being aware that we are getting ready to go somewhere, you would think that everybody was getting ready to go off on a holiday next week. That is the effect I have seen everywhere I have been in Canada. How in the world, with conditions like that obtaining throughout the country, can we have the phenomenal preparations for intercepting possible attacks as the minister assured us last year we had? I just cannot see that it is possible.
I must say that I am really worried about the situation, about the possibility of a lightning-like onslaught, something like what the Germans called a blitzkrieg-but this time it will be a blitzkrieg to the third or fourth power.
This afternoon the Prime Minister seemed to be a little aggrieved over the wording of the amendment moved by the opposition. He felt that it was not quite fair to suggest that His Excellency's advisers had failed to prepare adequately for the defence of Canada. He seemed to feel that they have not failed.
Let us examine the situation for a few minutes from the standpoint of the ordinary man in the street like myself who looks around the country and tries to form a conclusion from what he sees. Take milk, as an example. If there is one thing that Canada is eminently capable of producing, it is milk. I think there is probably only one other country in the British commonwealth that can produce milk to better advantage. What is happening in connection with milk? We are supposed to be in fine fettle for war; we are supposed to have plenty of supplies on hand. I noticed the following Canadian Press statement in the Ottawa Citizen of August 29, 1950;
DFC Claims Milk Shortage is Possibility
Toronto: Shortages of fresh milk in many Canadian cities during winter months may result from increasing competition of margarine with dairy products, the Dairy Fanners of Canada said yesterday.

In a brief to the conference of provincial ministers of agriculture, the council said a steady deterioration in the dairy situation would result in eventual milk shortages unless a ban were placed on the manufacture and sale of margarine.
The brief said butter takes about half the milk produced in Canada. If butter consumption decreased, the demand for milk would decrease proportionately. Less demand would mean smaller herds and the result would be shortage of fluid milk and higher prices in the low-yield winter months.
It may be said that is simply the working of natural forces, but if so they were natural forces which were brought into operation in large measure by this government. According to an article in the Ottawa Journal of the next day, August 30, 1950, the price of milk was to be increased one cent per quart on Friday. This has been referred to already today but let us refer to it again. This article reads:
The price of milk tb Ottawa consumers will go up one cent Friday, it was announced today.
Gordon Grier, president of the Ottawa valley milk producers, said a new agreement between local dairy farmers and distributors had been ratified by the Ontario milk control board, to be effective September 1.
It would mean Ottawa buyers would pay 19 cents a quart for milk on home delivery.
Reason for the increase, first since November of 1948, was given as increased cost of supplies, machinery, delivery equipment, dairy cattle, and feed, as well as increases recently granted to employees.
To local dairy farmers it would mean 15 cents more per hundred pounds of milk delivered at city plants-$4.20 instead of $4.05.
Consumer price adjustment would have to be made by the individual dairies, but it was presumed such products as buttermilk, chocolate milk, and other milk drinks would undergo a similar increase.
Well, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will ask, "What can we do about that? It is just a result of natural laws." Almost every one of these price increases is the direct result of governmental policy in this country. Increases in the cost of supplies, machinery, delivery equipment and so on, are all the result of governmental policy. And nothing in the world has been done to offset the adverse effects of the use of margarine on the dairy industry. The position of the dairy industry has always been more or less precarious, in my judgment, because of the fact that we have permitted so many of our choice dairy cattle to be taken to the United States. People will ask, "Well, how can you stop that?" If we really wanted to develop a dairy industry in Canada which would produce all the cheese our consumers could absorb, we would take steps to keep those good cows here, for they are just as valuable to us as to the people of the United States. Nothing is done, however, and you would think nothing could be done.

This is just a simple example of one thing. To the people of my constituency it is utterly incomprehensible that milk, which during the war was kept at a price of about 10 cents to the consumer, should now cost almost one hundred per cent more; and this in Canada, a land capable of literally flowing with milk and honey. Will anyone who faces facts try to argue that this indicates a proper discharge of the responsibilities of government? Something is terribly wrong somewhere; and the trouble is that the consumers, most of whom are existing in excruciating misery in an endeavour to make ends meet with their meagre incomes, are utterly bewildered and do not know what to do. I know many of them; I know their incomes, and I must confess that it remains an absolute mystery to me how they ever live. But it never seems to bother our government the slightest bit. This might as well be happening on the other side of the sun as far as the government are concerned. They think all is well, that there is no need to worry. They say, "Everything is fine; we are discharging our responsibility." I say conditions such as I have indicated are absolutely outrageous in a country like Canada.
Let us see what it means, Mr. Speaker. An average person should have a quart of milk a day, we are told; it is the best food anyone can have. In the case of a man, his wife and one child, if they are to have the milk they should have they must pay 57 cents a day or $17.10 a month. Just start figuring now. Then think of the cost of coal, which has been allowed to go up at an absolutely amazing rate. The price people must pay for coal is an utter scandal. It is $25 a ton right here in Ottawa, and that in a country where people must have coal. Rents have gone up and up until people are just sickened at the very thought of what they have to pay, and even at that in many cases they cannot get houses. Would anyone say conditions are such that the people have that calm confidence and equanimity which would fit them to enter into a war, and that the government has discharged its responsibilities for the defence of Canada? There must be some new way to use words if they can be made to mean the government has done all it should.
Now let us look at beef. Here again there are few countries on the face of the earth better equipped than Canada to produce this foodstuff, yet look at prices. They are so high that I imagine over sixty per cent of all the families in Canada have not tasted beef for a year. They just have not dared buy it. Even the price of lowly hamburger, to which people used to resort when they
The Address-Mr. Blackmore could not buy any other kind of meat, has gone up until it is impossible even to think about.

Let us now look at sugar. I happen to have quite a lot to do with sugar, because there are two large sugar factories in my constituency and another one is opening this year. Unfortunately, this is not due to any good work the government has done to encourage the development of that industry. Southern Alberta, Mr. Speaker, could be made the sugar bowl of Canada. Alberta, south of Calgary, can be made to produce all the sugar that Canada could possibly use, and could produce enough sugar so that we could supply great quantities of it to Britain and other needy countries during a war. Yet, in what condition do we find ourselves? During the last war we limited the consumption of sugar. In so far as I can gather we actually took sugar right out of Canada, took it away from the people. We had all sorts of stories about how cargoes of sugar were sunk by submarines, to encourage the people to deprive themselves of sugar.
What have we done since the last war in order to improve the situation? Nothing, nothing at all! What are we ready to do now? Nothing, nothing at all! We have allowed the price of sugar to go up seventy cents per hundred within the last week. There is


a magnificent contribution towards getting sugar for the people! Of course, the government will say, "Well, you have got to allow these industries to stand on their own feet." It would not be so bad having them stand on their own feet if the government and other agencies in the country would get off their back. To stand on their own feet, with all these people on their back, is quite a different matter. Canada is now able to produce, if she would only develop her capacity, far more than she needs in beet sugar alone. She actually is producing of beet sugar about one-quarter of her needs.
This afternoon we heard about the wonderful submarines the Russians are developing, and the great numbers of them. If we experienced trouble getting cargoes of sugar into Canada from some of the eastern islands during the last war, what do you suppose we shall have in this war? Yet the government acts as if nothing like that could occur. About the first month after war breaks out the government will discover something has gone wrong with the sugar supply. Then they will shake their hands and say, "What could we do about it?" "Who could have foreseen it?" Any fourteen-year-old boy in my constituency could foresee it.
We say we are ready for war, and that we have discharged our responsibility. Every member of this house saw what happened in the last war, as did every member in the government, in respect to sugar. Incidentally, I might just remind the government that when a sugar controller is appointed this time they should not select a man whose definite business is to destroy the beet sugar industry in Canada, and who has to be fought every inch of the way during the war to keep him from doing that. For goodness' sake select a man who wants to develop the sugar beet industry in Canada, and provide the people of Canada with sugar. In the last war, in 1942, we had a chance to put sugar factories in Canada which' would have been producing long before the war was over. Do you think we could get one of those sugar factories brought into Canada? No, not at all. Why? Because we had signed an illusory agreement in 1937 that we would not increase sugar production in Canada. We brilliant Canadians did a thing like that! I suppose that agreement is still in existence somewhere in the musty archives. Do we say this government has discharged its responsiblity? Whenever war is mentioned the first thing people worry about is sugar. We have not done a single thing to protect the sugar supply. The people who are able to buy sugar have bought it, and will continue to do so. The first thing we know, we shall have a shortage if war develops.

I would say it was a nine to one chance, and that is a very common-sense point of view. I believe there is a case to be made in support of the resolution of the leader of the opposition. As I have said already the government assumes far too little responsibility for helping the producers. We are still going on the assumption that the producers can stand on their own feet while the government stands not only on their backs but on the producers' feet as well. The government interferes with the producer in Canada today to such an extent that an ordinarily intelligent person would hardly believe it.

He is confronted with a harvest and yet all but eight bushels to the acre must be piled out on the stubble. Does the government accept the responsibility? Oh, no; the government cannot do that, but the farmer can! The farmer can meet all the vicissitudes of hailstorms, insects, droughts and every other type of hazard, the danger of falling prices and so forth. His shoulders are broad, so we will put all the responsibility upon him!
The situation confronting the farmers with whom I talked when I left my constituency was enough to put them into a state of despair. Of course the situation was aggravated by the strike, but let us bear in mind that even with the strike settled they will be delayed one week or ten days in securing cars to send their wheat out. The government incessantly tells us that price control is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. But the British North America Act does not refuse to allow the government to subsidize the provinces with enough money to enable them to take care of prices, just as the federal government itself did during the war. The Prime Minister laughs about that and thinks that it is a big joke; but the joke is going to be right on him just as sure as we are living. He thinks you cannot pay subsidies. But before he gets much further in public life in Canada he will discover a great many things about subsidies that he does not yet know.
We have got to a point today-and we cannot laugh this off; if we do, it is just evidence of great danger-where, if we are going to equalize the prices as between producer and consumer, we simply must use subsidies. If the provinces are going to take care of the matter of prices, they have got to have financial support from the central government which is able to give that financial support. That is all there is to it. It cost vast sums of money during the war to stabilize prices. We had the figures given, but I have not them at hand at the moment. It cost vast sums of money during the war to subsidize prices and keep the price structure stable, did it not? And the money was well spent. That has been granted time and again on the floor of the house and acknowledged by the ministers who had to do with it. The money will be just as well spent in that way today as it was during the war, because it will enable people to have something like stability, both as consumers and as producers. But there is no province that is able to supply the money that is necessary to maintain price stabilization similar to what was carried on during the war by the federal government. He does not worry about that at all! One of the reasons why we are having so much trouble is that there are so many people in responsible positions in our country who have never taken the trouble to think things right straight through so as to be consistent. The time has come for careful thinking right straight through and facing facts. If we do not do that, we are certainly going to fail to discharge our responsibilities to the country. I. now wish to deal just for a minute or two with the military aspects of our war effort. Thus far I have been dealing with the economic aspect. I make no pretence of being an authority of any kind with respect to war. In fact, I guess that I am probably a little bit better off if I do not know anything about wars in times past because we have to relearn everything for the war we are going to fight, apparently. I will tell you what effect the present military effort has on me. Our military effort gives me the same impression exactly as I had while we were in the "phony" war at the beginning of the last war. Everybody seemed to be living in a dense mist and groping. You remember, Mr. Speaker, the first six or eight months of that war? Then suddenly Germany hit us with the force of a catapult. We now seem to me to be in the midst of preparations for a phony war, or in the midst of a phony preparation. I hope I am entirely wrong.
At the beginning of the last war we had the assurance that all was well, that we were going to come through all right. It is true that we came through, but everybody knows how we did it!

Just let us face a few facts. What is the present Canadian force, counting every man who is trained and in uniform in Canada? What is that force in relation to Russia's colossal forces? It is pathetic. What is our present enlistment in relation to Russia's forces? Absolutely pathetic. We talk about the
12,000	who have applied to enlist. But what numbers should we have had apply if we are going to be prepared to fight a force like that of Russia? We have heard people say: Well, we cannot hope to fight Russia alone. No, we cannot. But if you have fifteen or sixteen countries, all as ill-prepared as we are, they will collectively have just about as much chance as we would have alone. That is just where the trouble is right now.
Get the facts and figures concerning the actual number of men the United States has today fit to go into the field. Then get the number that we have and the number that the other members of the so-called democracies-the free nations as we are pleased to call them-have, get the total number, put them all together and put them up against the power that Russia has!
Then, we are scattered all over the globe. I guess each of our associate nations is fighting a phony war like ourselves, and all offering the same excuses that we are offering. That is what I mean. I do not find any comfort in it at all. I do not want to be unduly harsh. I do not want to say anything that is unjustifiable.
I want to commend the Prime Minister for what he has done up to the present time. I think he has exercised admirable judgment in managing the country from the time this crisis occurred, but I would say this: For this country to be in the state of unpreparedness in which it is at the present time is a complete travesty. It is fantastic. With the manpower and the materials that we have in our country it is fantastic; that is all. With a nation the size of Russia, with the preparation she has, and everything we know about her, and the people that are guiding her, and the people who are following her, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) pointed out this afternoon, it is fantastic. I say it once more.
Let us bear in mind this, a thing I am sure every member of the government is aware of: There are about four fronts upon which Russia can strike, and it is evidence which I think supports the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the stand which he has taken. Canada is one of the major points, as we all know. Now, it would be brilliant to take all the fighting forces away from Canada and place them over there in Korea, would it not?
The Address-Mr. Knight I imagine the Russians would look upon that with the utmost complacency. There is Turkey Russia can strike, with the objective of going into Palestine and obtaining the oil east of Palestine, which I think we shall find is Russia's immediate objective, because her greatest need is oil, if I understand it aright.
Imagine getting all our forces concentrated in Korea while leaving that front exposed! There is western Europe, the importance of which Churchill has been trying desperately to impress upon us. His words have pretty well aroused the world to the seriousness of western Europe. Imagine taking all of Canada's forces and putting them in Korea, or in countries contiguous to Korea, and then having Russia make an attack on the western front! I wish that somebody who is able to think things through would give a talk to some of those United States extremists who are having so much to say! Meanwhile I think we are very fortuna-te that the government has been as wise as it has been in managing the war up to now; but nevertheless at the present time I have to indicate that I am not satisfied by any manner of means that the government in the absolute has come anywhere near discharging its responsibilities in respect of the defence of Canada.

I have perhaps not added to my personal popularity in many quarters by that declaration but I must proceed. Mr. Speaker, I shall tender my congratulations first of all, as is usual, to those who moved and seconded the motion on the address. The custom of doing that is a pleasant convention for us here and perhaps a useful one, to the extent that it tends to promote personal harmony amongst those whose political convictions align them up on opposite sides of the house or more correctly in various political camps, who can yet, as we have proved, work together towards the common weal in a spirit of mutual tolerance and respect, in a spirit which is an essential condition to a successful democracy.

The Address-Mr. Knight
We were summoned here for this special session under circumstances of greatest import to this nation. We have emerged from the immediate domestic crisis, to the extent that our transportation system is again in full operation, into a period when negotiations will continue in an atmosphere which I think has been bettered considerably, and certainly has been cleared. It must be the hope of all of us that complete agreement may be speedily reached, and that there will not need to be invoked that element of compulsion in arbitration which most of us in the house would deplore.
The other domestic crisis, in addition to the rail strike, which I found engaging the minds of those at home with whom I talked was the inflation which has taken place in this country, and which is robbing the people of the purchasing power of such money as they have left to them, and is sending the cost of living in a steady spiral up; and just as steady is the rising demand that this government do something about it. If in our preoccupation with other matters we neglect this problem, we may wake up to realize that it has already attained proportions in which the whole economic equilibrium of the nation may be threatened.
In passing, let me say that most people with whom I had the opportunity to speak thought that there was sufficient justification in this problem and in the Korean crisis for the calling of parliament not just a few days ago, but many weeks ago; and it was felt that if parliament had been called, as in my opinion it should have been, in connection with the Korean situation, that the railroad strike either would not have occurred, or it would have been settled in a day or two as events later proved that it could have been, rather than that the whole country should have been kept as it was for a period of some ten days in uncertainty, suspense and economic danger.
With all these problems there has been an element of indecision and pussyfooting on the part of the government, a sort of wait-and-see attitude, a Micawber-like attitude of waiting until perchance something might turn up, which would do away with the necessity of clear and decisive action.
As to the Korean question, which is the next problem on my list, we must face the fact that there is in the minds of the people in our constituencies of all political groups some confusion, and indeed some misgiving. I think someone perhaps should attempt to analyse here the causes of some of those misgivings. I am glad that the Secretary of


State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said some things in his speech yesterday which should lessen the misgivings which I heard expressed.
Let me say to begin with that our own group in the House of Commons, and I think the vast majority of our followers in this country, favour the idea of group police action against any aggressor.
What are some of those misgivings which I have mentioned? One hears them among the people. What are they thinking about? What are they saying? What they are saying concerns each and every one of us. Let us not despise the opinions of minorities. They are the opinions of honest and sincere people seeking to emerge from the grey shadow of a partial conflict, of an uneasy cold war, hoping to emerge into the light of day, of peace, and hoping not to be enveloped by the dark clouds of a total war itself. They want peace. And let me hasten to add that I am not referring here to people in what are known as the various peace fronts, either the innocent or the sinister varieties. We must have peace, but it must be a peace which can be enjoyed by free men.
To get back to my misgivings: the greatest fear I have heard expressed by most people with whom I have talked has been the fear of the solidification of the antagonism widely held among Asiatics against outside interference of any kind, even of the United Nations. This antagonism can be attributed, among other things, to the failure of some nations to recognize the government of China at the time it should have been recognized, and before there was any question of duress, any question of making that recognition an element in a bargain. By failing to recognize that government-and recognition does not involve any love for its system-we have thrown to Stalin the free gift of a propaganda weapon, in the use of which he is showing considerable proficiency. By that I mean that he is now posing as the great defender of the Asiatic people, as their main advocate in the cause of recognition.
Let me say here-and this is only a personal view-that I am not sure in my own mind that what was morally right a year ago is morally wrong now. My Liberal friends across the way will not like that statement, since it implies that the government which they follow so assiduously made a mistake at that time. But let me remind them that it is not the first time my hon. friends on the Liberal side have made a mistake. That fact came vividly to my mind a few moments ago

as I sat and listened to the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I remembered how my Liberal friends, and also my Progressive Conservative friends who sit to my right, applauded that speech to the echo tonight. That was the speech of a man whom a year or two ago, and particularly before the last election, they were characterizing openly as a communist while being a member of this group.

My friends perhaps did not make the direct accusation, but they allowed the few people who had that opinion to retain it and, so far as I know, did little or nothing to contradict it.
The second point to remember is that even liberation can involve tremendous tragedy for those native people when such liberation involves the use of large-scale bombing. The danger is that military action, if carried far enough, and used as the sole instrument of such liberation, may defeat its very purpose. I underline what many of my colleagues have said before, that military action must be accompanied by economic aid, by the raising of the standard of living of the Asiatic people, and by showing to them a sincere and genuine desire to help them, not in any selfish way but for the very sake of friendship. Otherwise those peoples may even by their free choice be prepared to barter their freedom for subsistence and to look askance at those whom, in their limited view, they may blame for the actual destruction.
I was glad to hear the minister's statement in regard to Formosa, and to learn that the two questions relating to Korea and Formosa are to be kept separate. The people are worried lest we fail to make that distinction in regard to those two places. I am glad we have a policy of our own in that connection. Let us back up the United Nations policy, the collective policy, by all means; but let us not become satellites of any other nation in regard to our views on that or any other question.
Many people-and I confess that in this at least I am one of them.-know with some chagrin that when we did decide to say, with a collective voice, "Thus far and no farther", and when we did decide to erect a limit and a dividing wall, Chiang Kai-shek was the first reactionary to crouch behind that wall and to claim its protection.
The last cause of danger I shall mention, or at least the last I shall draw to the attention of the house tonight, is the apparent lack of program of this government for the reha-
The Address-Mr. Knight bilitation and recovery of the Asiatic people generally-and I am not speaking particularly in this instance of Korea-and a rehabilitation from what the minister described yesterday as a swamp of poverty which, in his estimation, must be drained off if we are to have fertile fields in which democratic ideas may grow. The government is inclined to say a lot and to promise a lot. Perhaps like some of our good neighbours, they do not take their commitments seriously enough. They do not always fulfil them. In this instance I think it is vital that we make these commitments, and that we fulfil them in our own interests, if not for any more altruistic reason.
We have been told and we believe that we must be strong. It is a hard decision to make, with some of the beliefs we hold, when we realize that we may have again to resort to war for any cause or for any purpose. If the occasion arises we shall not shrink from it. We shall not shrink from it if it involves action on the part of the United Nations, to which we are pledged.
Under the circumstances in which we find ourselves we will have to expand our armed services. We must, too, expand our industrial plant, its capacity and production. We must decentralize industry as opportunity offers itself. Decentralization in these days of the atomic bomb must certainly be a necessity obvious to all. While we are doing these things which have a relation to war we must not neglect those things which have a relation to our own economic well-being. We must produce as much housing as possible; we must raise the morale of our people by eliminating injustices; we must not allow our social services, our educational services, our medical services or the scale on which we provide for our older people to become the first casualties of war, something which experience has shown to happen. This is a great task we have set for ourselves. It is the responsibility of this people; it is the responsibility of this government. It is a great task but one that Canada has proved in the past that she has the ability and the capacity to undertake.
I think we Canadians have of late cast off that inferiority complex with which we have been somewhat bedevilled perhaps through no fault of our own but rather as a consequence of our history. That inferiority complex has been to our disadvantage in connection with matters such as the creation of art and literature as well as in taking our place among the nations of the world. Both last year and this year we made moves which proclaimed to all the independence of this

The Address-Mr. Knight nation from other nations, but an independence which does not preclude association of the warmest and friendliest character with other nations of the commonwealth and, indeed with other nations of the world.
If the minister of immigration has anything to say I wish he would say it now as it rather annoys me to have him making signs without speech. I take it from his gestures that he is indicating that I still have five minutes to speak. Perhaps as I have been interrupted, Your Honour will allow me to call it eleven o'clock and thus put both the
minister and myself out of our misery at one stroke. Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
